Even after the Department of Transport Management announced a 2 percent reduction in inter-provincial public transport fares effective from early last month, passengers are still paying the inflated price. Thanks to weak market regulation and ineffective monitoring, the public continues to bear the brunt of price hikes.

The government should not leave people to fight surging prices of daily essentials alone; it must take visible actions and come up with long-term solutions to alleviate the public woe. To begin with, it can withdraw its revenue-collecting policies such as 5 percent VAT on household electricity consumption above 50 units and 13 percent VAT on non-household use. Such policies are detrimental and will only erode trust in the government. Additionally, regular monitoring activities alone will play a big role in curbing the artificial surge in prices in the market. As the festival season approaches, the need for stronger market oversight should be dealt with urgency. Activities like spreading exaggerated predictions of food and gas shortages must be contained.

A resilient agricultural system, which is the backbone of our economy, is another essential, sustainable component for managing price hikes and reducing Nepal’s dependence on imported food and agricultural inputs. For this, investment in irrigation, storage facilities, rural roads and cold-chain infrastructure is necessary. By addressing these needs, the state can instil hope among citizens that it is committed to protecting their well-being.

articles.title: This family-run Prague restaurant is introducing Czech diners to Nepal
articles.summary:
A little piece of Nepal sits in Prague, the capital of the Czech Republic, where a giant mural of the Buddha welcomes visitors. Walking inside, Czech diners can be seen tucking into plates of an ‘all-you-can buffet’ that runs from 11 am to 2 pm, Monday to Friday.

Around them hang traditional Nepali musical instruments—a full Naumati Baja set—turning the restaurant into something that feels as much like a cultural centre as an eatery.

This is Lumbini-Indická a Nepálská Restaurace, a family-run Nepali and Indian restaurant in Prague’s Žižkov district. For husband-and-wife duo Baikuntha Rayamajhi and Anjana Rayamajhi, who jointly run the establishment, serving food, they say, is only part of their mission.

Just as important, they say, is preserving and promoting Nepali culture thousands of kilometres away from home.

Although the eatery was established about eight years ago, the couple took over its management more than two years ago. Baikuntha says the opportunity came unexpectedly.

“I jokingly asked the owner if he wanted to sell the restaurant,” he recalls. “We negotiated as a joke, but eventually the deal actually happened.”

Years of organising community events convinced him that a restaurant could be more than just a place to eat. He saw it as a space where Nepalis could come together while Czech diners discovered Nepal’s cuisine and traditions.

Today, Lumbini-Indická a Nepálská Restaurace serves familiar Nepali dishes such as momo, dal bhat and thali alongside Indian favourites, attracting Nepali, Indian and Czech customers alike.

But the walls reveal another side of the restaurant’s identity. The collection of traditional musical instruments is not simply for decoration.

Since 2013, Baikuntha has led a Naumati Baja team that performs at weddings and community events across the Czech Republic and occasionally elsewhere in Europe.

“My wife and I also sing dohori,” he says. “We have our own performing team with musical instruments and a sound system.”

Anjana Rayamajhi shares both the business and the stage with her husband. While helping manage the day-to-day operations of the restaurant, she also performs traditional Nepali songs during cultural events, making music a natural extension of their family life.

Whenever Nepali artists visit the Czech Republic, many of their programmes are hosted inside the restaurant.

Baikuntha Rayamajhi’s involvement in cultural activities extends well beyond the restaurant. He is the founding president of the International Nepali Artists Society (INAS) Czech Republic.

“When I started organising programmes, there weren’t many Nepali cultural events here,” he says. “Now there are many more people involved.”

For many Czech diners, Lumbini-Indická a Nepálská Restaurace is their first introduction to Nepal. They arrive for the food but often leave having encountered something more—a glimpse of the country’s music and traditions.

For Nepalis living in Prague, meanwhile, the restaurant offers a familiar space where language, culture and community come together.

As Nepali migration to Europe continues to grow (an estimated 450,000–500,000 Nepali nationals live across Europe), restaurants like this are increasingly serving purposes that extend far beyond business. They become gathering places, performance venues and informal cultural institutions.

At Lumbini-Indická a Nepálská Restaurace, an ‘all-you-can-eat buffet’ may bring customers through the door. But it is the sounds of the madal, the melodies of dohori and the warmth of a Nepali family welcoming guests that leave the strongest impression.

articles.title: Movie review: In ‘Hope’, a monster emerges, but the mystery fades
articles.summary:
The first thing ‘Hope’ destroys is certainty.

A cow lies mutilated on a regular road, its body marked by deep claw wounds. The police think it's a tiger. The hunters insist the animal wandered down from the North. The villagers cling to explanations they already understand because the alternative is far more chilling. Na Hong-jin has always been fascinated by the moment ordinary logic begins to collapse, and ‘Hope’ spends nearly an hour stretching that moment as far as it can.

For a director whose last feature, ‘The Wailing’ (2016), became one of Korean cinema's defining horror films, ‘Hope’ arrives carrying unusual expectations. It is reportedly the most expensive Korean film ever made, features an international cast that includes Michael Fassbender and Alicia Vikander, and marks Na's return after a decade-long absence. The scale is bigger than anything he has attempted before. Surprisingly, what makes ‘Hope’ compelling has very little to do with its size.

Set in the coastal settlement of Hope Harbor near the Korean Demilitarized Zone, the film follows police chief Bum-seok (Hwang Jung-min), who is called to investigate what appears to be an isolated animal attack. By the time he returns to town, entire streets have been reduced to rubble. Buildings have collapsed. Cars have been hurled across roads. Bodies lie scattered where ordinary life had existed only hours before.

Na refuses to show the cause immediately. Instead, he builds suspense through absence. Every destroyed storefront, every terrified witness and every frantic chase expands the creature in the audience's imagination. The longer the monster remains unseen, the more convincing it becomes. Horror has always relied on this principle, but few contemporary blockbusters trust it for this long.

The decision allows cinematographer Hong Kyung-pyo to turn destruction into something strangely elegant. His camera glides through chaos rather than chasing it. Long tracking shots map the town with remarkable clarity, allowing viewers to understand not only where the action is taking place but also what has been lost. There is no frantic editing attempting to manufacture excitement. The filmmaking trusts movement more than speed.

That patience extends beyond the action.

Hope Harbor never feels like another anonymous disaster zone waiting to be demolished. Before the aliens arrive, Na quietly establishes a community held together by kinship rather than convenience. Everyone knows everyone else. Characters introduce themselves through family relationships before occupations. People argue, tease, gossip and panic like neighbours who have spent decades sharing the same streets. Even Bum-seok's stubborn determination to rescue his cousin feels less like heroic obligation than something instinctive within a community where blood ties continue to define identity.

This attention to locality becomes one of the film's most interesting qualities. The border setting, the faded propaganda signs warning against North Korean infiltrators, the absence of mobile phones and the analogue texture of daily life create a world that feels suspended somewhere between history and memory. Although Na deliberately leaves the time period ambiguous, the film remains deeply rooted in a recognisably Korean rural landscape. That grounding makes the intrusion of the impossible genuinely unsettling.

It also makes the creature reveal unexpectedly disappointing.

The problem isn't simply that the visual effects occasionally look unfinished. It is that the digital creature never belongs within the tactile world Na has spent so much time constructing. The buildings feel real. The roads feel lived in. The dust, debris and blood all possess convincing physical weight. The monster often doesn't. Instead of disrupting reality, it seems detached from it.

The irony is difficult to ignore. Few directors understand the power of suggestion as well as Na Hong-jin, yet ‘Hope’ gradually abandons the very restraint that makes its opening act so effective.

As the story expands, its mythology does too. Additional creatures appear. International stars emerge beneath layers of digital effects. The narrative begins reaching for something closer to large-scale science fiction than contained creature horror. None of these developments are inherently misguided. The problem is that they dilute the tension rather than deepen it.

The film becomes less interested in mystery once it starts answering questions.

At 160 minutes, ‘Hope’ also struggles with rhythm. Na has always allowed his stories room to breathe, but here the breathing occasionally turns into wandering. Several comic detours outstay their welcome, while repeated action sequences begin competing with one another instead of building naturally towards a climax.

Still, dismissing the film on those grounds alone would overlook what Na continues to achieve even during its weaker stretches.

Few contemporary action directors stage movement with this much confidence. A prolonged highway chase near the film's conclusion demonstrates remarkable control over geography and momentum. Vehicles overturn, buildings collapse and bodies are thrown through space with startling precision, yet the action does not become visually incoherent. Even when the computer-generated imagery fails to convince, the choreography remains consistently inventive.

The performances help sustain that energy.

Hwang Jung-min gives Bum-seok an appealing mixture of authority and vulnerability. He is introduced as a police chief eager to maintain control, yet much of the film quietly undermines that image. Bum-seok panics. He hesitates. He makes poor decisions. Hwang never attempts to disguise these flaws, allowing the character's fear to become one of the film's more recognisable human qualities.

Jung Ho-yeon is equally memorable as officer Sung-ae. Armed with increasingly absurd firepower and an unwavering confidence, she provides much of the film's comic momentum without becoming reduced to comic relief. Her presence prevents ‘Hope’ from sinking beneath the weight of its own seriousness.

More interestingly, Na gradually complicates the familiar humans-versus-monsters narrative. Without revealing too much, the film eventually begins shifting its perspective in ways that unsettle the audience's loyalties. Violence that initially appears justified slowly becomes more ambiguous. Fear begins to resemble prejudice. The creatures themselves acquire an emotional dimension that complicates their role as simple invaders.

It is an intriguing direction, though one the screenplay explores only briefly before returning to spectacle.

Perhaps that is the film's defining contradiction. It repeatedly gestures towards a richer emotional and moral complexity, but it is also determined to remain an unapologetic blockbuster. Sometimes those ambitions coexist. Sometimes they pull against one another.

The film's weaknesses stand out precisely because its strengths are so persuasive. The first hour demonstrates extraordinary confidence in atmosphere, pacing and visual storytelling. It is filmmaking that trusts silence, implication and uncertainty. The later sections rely more heavily on explanation, digital spectacle and scale, becoming progressively less distinctive as they grow larger.

Still, even at its most uneven, ‘Hope’ never feels anonymous.

There is too much personality in the filmmaking for that. Na stages action with an inventiveness rarely seen in contemporary studio spectacles. He understands how to transform ordinary spaces into sites of extraordinary tension. More importantly, he understands that monsters become frightening not because of how they look, but because of what they force people to reveal about themselves.

For much of its running time, ‘Hope’ remembers that. One only wishes it had trusted that instinct until the very end.

articles.title: How Arya Nishaant uses AI as a catalyst for growth
articles.summary:
Creating efficiency

Artificial intelligence has become an invaluable tool in my journey of learning, creating, and growing. I don’t see AI as something that replaces my work but something that amplifies it. It allows me to work more efficiently. There are, of course, things it cannot do; it cannot replace the person you are, but it is helpful nonetheless.

Public appearances

Throughout my Miss Nepal journey, AI has been a trusted learning companion. It has helped me prepare for interviews, refine my speeches, and challenge my perspectives by encouraging me to think more deeply about my values, my advocacy, and the impact I hope to create. Rather than giving me answers, it has helped me ask better questions and articulate my own voice with greater clarity and confidence.

AI as an assistant

Professionally and academically, I use AI to organise ideas, simplify complex information, conduct research, and enhance presentations and written communication. By reducing the time spent on repetitive tasks, it allows me to dedicate more energy to meaningful work, strategic thinking, and human connection.

AI as a friend

Beyond work, AI fuels my curiosity. Whether I am exploring business and finance, discovering new books, seeking creative inspiration for art and fashion, or simply learning about the world, it encourages me to remain a lifelong learner. Every conversation becomes an opportunity to expand my perspective and deepen my understanding.

articles.title: As AI-generated covers spread, Nepali musicians fight to reclaim their voices
articles.summary:
On June 29, singer Sugam Pokharel posted a status on Facebook with a stern warning. He issued an immediate demand for the removal of unauthorised AI-generated content utilising his or other artists’ works. “If you ignore this request,” he wrote, “we will have no choice but to bring you within the jurisdiction of the law, wherever you may be, in Nepal or anywhere else in the world.” The status included screenshots of AI covers of his originals uploaded on Youtube and Tiktok.

Pokharel says he first learned his songs were being run through AI months earlier, not from any platform notification but from listeners who told him directly.

He says he is not opposed to AI itself. He uses apps like Suno, the AI music creation platform, in his own creative process. He feeds in his lyrics and compositions to the app to sketch out arrangements before handing them to a producer. For an arranger, the work would take hours, if not days. Now it can be done at a fraction of the cost and time, he says.

What Pokharel objects to is the unauthorised use of his voice, melodies and lyrics. This distinction—AI as a creative tool versus a means of misappropriation—is a hot topic in Nepal’s music industry today.

The debate has reached law enforcement. Bimal Adhikari, who runs the label Bhavna Music Solution, recently took his complaint to Nepal Police’s Cyber Bureau. He first noticed songs under his label being altered and re-uploaded about six or seven months ago and initially assumed the trend would fade out on its own. It didn’t. His work was relabelled under different names and traded commercially; by the time he acted, somewhere between 40 and 50 of his songs had been altered with the help of AI, several traced to a single person operating 10 to 12 YouTube channels.

Adhikari is precise about what makes this different from AI music in general. “Even if a song is made by AI, the melody is 100 percent the melody I created,” he says. “The lyrics are also the same. It isn’t an ‘AI-generated song’. It is my composition and my words.”

Deputy Superintendent of Police Gajendra Acharya said the Bureau categorises complaints based on the nature of the offence rather than under a dedicated AI music category. As a result, it was unable to provide statistics on AI music-related complaints.

Adhikari adds he worries about what comes next. Automated copyright-detection systems, he fears, could eventually flag original artists for infringement on their own material, while the anonymous channels that triggered the confusion disappear and resurface under new names, leaving the strike behind on the real artist’s account.

Adhikari has so far filed an individual copyright complaint against around 95 YouTube channels for unauthorised use of his content. Many of the cases were later settled after those responsible apologised, acknowledged their wrongdoing and removed the offending content.

Both Pokharel and Adhikari trace part of the problem back to the law itself. Nepal’s Copyright Act was passed in 2002. Pokharel argues that it was never formulated to anticipate voice cloning. “If someone takes your house or your property, paints it a different colour, and then puts it on the market to sell, that’s illegal, isn’t it?” Pokharel says. Noting that current prime minister, Balendra Shah, is himself a musician, Pokharel says the Ministry of Communication and Information Technology should prioritise updating the laws.

Not everyone experiencing the shift sees only loss in it. Santosh Chapagain, who owns Pass Café in Kathmandu, has played AI-generated music for eight or nine months now, a habit he traces to the period around the Gen Z movement. “Music is life for musicians,” Chapagain says. “But for us, music is for entertainment, for peace of mind.” He adds, “We play whichever music makes us happy.” From devotional songs in the morning to timeless classics or rap, he plays it all in his cafe. His customers have noticed this change, some have remarked that he used to play the old songs before, but he says there has been no real pushback, and he has found uses for the technology beyond convenience: AI-generated bhajans, or turning a sad Dashain song into a happy one on request.

According to Nepal’s laws, and laws around the world, Chapagain says, using someone’s copyrighted work without permission is illegal. He would support a labelling requirement if regulators introduced one for cafés, he says. But he doesn’t see the original and the AI version as competing versions. “Original is original. Gold is still gold,” he said. “Its price changes over time, but its value remains.”

Utsaha Joshi (Uniq Poet), an artist who works with AI tools directly, says the popular image of how the music actually gets made—one prompt, one upload—is wrong. It starts with a human vision: humming a melody, writing lyrics, sometimes playing and recording instruments before any prompting begins. Only after that groundwork comes AI-assisted production, which includes prompting, re-prompting, separating stems, and assembling the result “brick by brick.” What gets automated, in this account, is manual execution, not creative direction.

If a generation draws on an artist’s own data, Joshi argues, that artist should be paid for it, however small the amount, which would require music models to be trained alongside a genuine attribution system and a clear opt-out for artists.

An AI-created cover version of Sugam Pokharel’s much-loved song “Pheri Tyo Din”.The question—how to make AI’s use of an artist’s voice visible, if not yet compensable—is what a new global labelling initiative is also attempting to address, at least on paper. Announced by the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI) and the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA), alongside other organisations including the Grammy Awards’ organisers, the voluntary framework introduces two labels: “Created by AI,” for content where the main vocals or lead instrumental tracks were substantially AI-generated, and “AI-Assisted,” for human-made music that used AI for specific elements, with a requirement to disclose clearly if a person did not perform the main vocals or instruments.

Some platforms are already moving. Deezer now automatically tags AI-generated uploads and reports that nearly half of new submissions to the platform are AI-generated, with a detection system it says is 99.8 percent accurate. An Apple Music official said earlier this year that more than a third of new uploads to the platform are fully AI-generated. Spotify introduced a “Spotify-verified” label last April aimed at confirming official artist content and curbing AI impersonation. The Digital Media Association, which represents Apple Music, Amazon Music and Spotify, has welcomed the framework, saying it will give listeners clearer information and strengthen the metadata attached to AI content.

None of this is specific to Nepal. No domestic streaming service or regulator has proposed a comparable disclosure system, even as Nepali listeners are, by several accounts here, already encountering unlabelled AI-generated music daily: in cafés, on buses, at devotional gatherings, without being told.

Suresh Manandhar, an AI scientist, sees the same divide from a different angle. In his view, AI has genuinely lowered the barrier to making music. From cutting the cost and time of composing and writing lyrics for artists who already create, while opening music-making to people who couldn’t previously afford it. “That is a very positive effect,” he said. The problem, he said, isn’t the tool. It’s that someone who is skilled with the tool but isn’t a creator can take an original artist’s lyrics or music and “twist it into their own creation,” which is where questions of ownership and attribution—still unresolved in Nepal—begin.

Asked where the line should sit between creative use and unauthorised imitation, Manandhar reached for an analogy from his own field. “Just as we provide citations and references in academic work, any AI-generated content should be clearly labelled as ‘AI-Generated,’” he said. Voice cloning, in his view, is the clearest case for mandatory labelling and attribution. Lyrics are trickier, since reworking existing lyrics or melodies into something new predates AI, Hindi film songs have long borrowed from English or Nepali ones. He argued that the ownership rules therefore shouldn’t change just because AI was involved: if a person turns one set of lyrics into another using an AI tool, the work, and the ownership, is still theirs, and the legal question should be judged exactly as it would be without AI in the picture.

But Manandhar also cautioned that labelling alone won’t settle what Nepali musicians are asking for, because “what exactly we are protecting” is not one thing. Lyrics, musical style, audio-visual style, and an artist’s cloned voice each need their own rule, he said, rather than a single blanket policy. He offered his own hypothesis: turning a Narayan Gopal song into a rap track. That transformation was possible before AI—it would simply have taken longer by hand—so the financial and intellectual ownership of the original hit, he argued, should be treated no differently whether AI was used to do it or not.

Looking ahead, Manandhar expects the technology to move from a production shortcut to something closer to a collaborator. Within the next year, he said, artists are likely to work with AI agents that hold a working knowledge of everything they’ve previously created, letting a musician describe a mood, an instrument, or a visual setting and have the assistant draft variations to refine into a finished song—an extension, he said, of what people are already doing informally with short-form drafts on platforms like TikTok.

For now, the burden of flagging AI-generated music falls on artists themselves, checking their own catalogues, filing their own complaints, writing their own warnings on Facebook.

Adhikari says his own case is resolved, for now. But he does not think it is over. “Other friends have thousands of songs that are being used purely for trade,” he said. “I believe this issue will be raised by many others in the coming days.”

articles.title: Australia tightens student visa rules, rejects 64 percent of Nepali applications
articles.summary:
Australia has rejected around 64 percent of offshore student visa applications from Nepal, marking the highest rejection rate recorded for Nepali applicants, according to official data.

The surge in visa refusals comes after the Australian government tightened its screening process for international students amid concerns over migration levels, housing pressures and the integrity of the education system.

Australia categorises countries under an “Evidence Level” risk framework to determine the level of scrutiny applied during visa processing. Education sector insiders say Nepal was recently moved to “Level 3”, the highest-risk category, from “Level 2” following a government review conducted several months ago.

The impact has been most severe in the vocational education and training (VET) sector, which traditionally attracts students seeking shorter and more affordable courses. Nearly 90 percent of Nepali applications for VET courses have been rejected, with only 56 of 549 applicants receiving visas, according to recent statistics.

Around 60,000 Nepali students are currently enrolled in Australian institutions. Of them, about 56,000 are existing students, while roughly 4,000 are new arrivals.

Data from Australia’s Department of Home Affairs shows a sharp decline in new student arrivals from Nepal. Between January and May this year, only 2,700 of 7,500 offshore applicants from Nepal were granted visas. During the same period last year, 7,167 of 8,028 applicants received approvals.

The uncertainty surrounding visa approvals, combined with rising application costs, has discouraged many prospective students. Applicants currently have to pay an application fee of A$2,500 (approximately Rs260,000), which is non-refundable even if the visa is rejected.

Sanjeev Pandey, a Sydney-based lawyer, said Australia had welcomed a large number of international students after the Covid-19 pandemic, but authorities later became concerned about patterns of students changing courses and extending their stay without completing their original programmes.

“The government may have also tightened student visa rules to address growing employment and housing pressures,” Pandey said.

The stricter visa regime has raised concerns among education consultancies and smaller institutions that rely heavily on international enrolments.

Khagendra Satyal, international business development manager at Central Australian College, said the decline in student arrivals had significantly affected the sector.

“Visas are now granted only after assessing what positive contributions an international student can make to Australia in the long run,” Satyal said. “Students applying from Nepal need to understand this shift.”

The immigration crackdown also comes amid growing political pressure in Australia over migration. Analysts say the rise of politicians with hardline positions on immigration, including Pauline Hanson, has contributed to a broader political push for tighter controls.

Lawyer Pandey said the tougher environment has affected not only prospective students but also those already in Australia. Renewing student visas, switching back to student visas after completing post-study work arrangements, and bringing spouses as dependants have all become more difficult, he said.

Obtaining permanent residency has also become significantly more challenging compared with previous years.

Despite the tightening measures, Nepal remains one of the largest sources of international students in Australia. Government data shows Nepali students account for around nine percent of Australia's international student population, making Nepal the third-largest source country.

articles.title: Budget-friendly places for Nepali students in Ohio
articles.summary:
Athens is a small, scenic college town in southeastern Ohio, shaped largely by Ohio University and its energetic student community. Surrounded by rolling hills, rivers and forests, the town combines historic streets, local businesses and easy access to nature.

The university campus, downtown shops and restaurants are concentrated within a compact area, making daily life manageable without a car. Ohio University students can also use Athens Public Transit free of charge, while nearby trails and forests provide inexpensive options for hiking and outdoor recreation.

Because Athens is a relatively small town, the number of professional internships available locally can be limited. Although Ohio University hosts career fairs and attracts employers from across the country, students may need to look beyond Athens or relocate temporarily for specialised opportunities.

Oxford is a compact, classic college town in southwestern Ohio, built almost entirely around Miami University at its core. Red-brick Georgian buildings, leafy streets and a walkable uptown give it a traditional campus-town character.

The compact layout means campus, uptown restaurants, shops and student housing are all within easy walking distance. The town is also considered quite safe, and Miami University's strong sense of community brings a steady calendar of campus events, traditions and activities that keep student life active without needing to travel elsewhere.

The town's economy is heavily tied to the university, so it can feel quiet or emptied out during breaks and summer months when students are away.

ColumbusColumbus is Ohio's capital and largest city, and it's where The Ohio State University, one of the biggest campuses in the country, is situated. Rather than a self-contained college town, Columbus functions as a full city with sprawling neighborhoods, a job market, and student population that's just one part of a much bigger urban picture.

Pros:Living costs stay reasonable even with everything a major city offers, and students get real exposure to internships and employers across finance, tech, healthcare and government without having to leave town.

Cons:The scale of the city brings more traffic and scattered housing options, so building a close community takes a bit more intention than it would in a smaller town.

Cincinnati is moving to universities like the University of Cincinnati and Xavier University. The city has 300,000 people and many residential areas.

Pros:The city offers people a diverse job market. It is home to many consumer goods, finance and healthcare companies. The cost of living is on the lower end for cities of this size.

Cons:Despite its universities, the city is not generally considered a college town. Younger residents have to actively seek college-town experiences since it is not part of city life. The city is also not walkable.

Toledo is Ohio’s fourth largest city, sitting on the edge of Lake Erie. It is a city of 600,000 people and home to the University of Toledo.

Pros: The University of Toledo sits at the centre of city life. It is the biggest school in town and also the town's biggest employer. Students have a solid pipeline to work experience and internships.

Cons: As a Rust Belt city, its growth has been stagnant over the years. And despite its size, it is considered to be falling behind the other major metros in Ohio.

Based on conversations with local Nepali students in Ohio.

articles.title: Migrant workers can strike under new Qatari labour law
articles.summary:
The Qatari government has introduced a conditional right for migrant workers to stage legal strikes as part of amendments to the country’s labour law.

Under the revised law, workers can go on strike for up to six working days after notifying their employer and the Ministry of Labour in writing, but only if a labour dispute cannot be resolved through negotiation, conciliation or mediation. The provision was introduced through Qatar’s Law No 9 of 2026, which amended the 2004 Labour Law (Law No 14) to strengthen workers’ rights and welfare.

The amended law requires companies with 100 or more employees to establish joint committees made up of management and worker representatives. The committees are intended to improve workplace dialogue, strengthen consultation and help resolve disputes before they escalate.

The reforms also introduce tougher penalties for labour violations. Employers that breach wage protection regulations may face suspension of ministry services, while the Labour Dispute Resolution Committee has been formally authorised to conduct virtual hearings. Recruitment agencies and companies involved in hiring violations may face fines ranging from QAR3,000 to QAR25,000. One Qatari riyal is equivalent to Rs41.66.

Workers exercising their right to strike will not be entitled to wages during the strike period. The law also allows companies to dismiss without notice workers who organise illegal or unjustified strikes without following the required procedures or who disrupt business operations through such actions.

Companies that fail to establish mandatory joint committees may face fines ranging from QAR2,000 to QAR5,000.

Qatar has also strengthened enforcement of its Wage Protection System. The amended law gives the labour ministry greater authority to take action against employers that delay or fail to pay salaries, including suspending services, imposing administrative measures and applying regulatory penalties against repeat offenders.

If a company repeatedly violates wage rules or triggers collective disputes because of unpaid salaries, other companies under the same ownership may also face penalties. The ministry may publish the names of non-compliant companies on its website.

Workers who remain unpaid can request a change of employer or terminate their contracts, with repatriation costs to be covered by the employer.

The Labour Dispute Resolution Committee’s new authority to conduct virtual hearings means workers no longer need to be physically present to pursue labour cases. Employers, workers and verified witnesses can now participate in proceedings online.

Workers must first register disputes with the ministry. Cases are referred to the dispute resolution committee only when efforts to settle them through negotiation fail. Agreements reached through ministry-led mediation will have the status of legally enforceable documents.

The amended law also increases penalties for recruitment-related violations.

Recruitment agencies can be fined between QAR3,000 and QAR25,000 for hiring workers without ministry approval for employment contracts, processing recruitment before mandatory medical examinations or committing other administrative and recruitment-related violations.

Qatari recruitment agencies generally recruit workers in partnership with manpower agencies in Nepal, although some employers also hire directly through Nepali firms.

The new rules also require workers seeking employment in designated technical and professional occupations to obtain certificates confirming that they have completed required training and passed examinations at ministry-approved centres before starting work.

Meanwhile, Qatar has extended the non-compete period, during which an employee can be restricted from joining a competing company after leaving a job, from one year to two years. The change restores a provision that existed before 2020.

If an employee has access to sensitive client information, trade secrets or confidential company data, an employer can prevent them from joining a competitor for up to two years after the termination of employment.

The labour law amendments are aimed at modernising Qatar’s labour market, improving regulatory oversight and creating a more flexible and competitive employment system in line with the Qatar National Vision 2030. Some provisions will require additional decrees and executive regulations before they come into full effect.

“These reforms represent significant shifts that will heavily impact employers, workers, recruitment agencies and the dispute resolution system alike,” Krishna Panthi, president of the Non-Resident Nepali Association Qatar, told Kantipur.

articles.title: 67 Nepalis died in Japan over ten months, 25 killed themselves
articles.summary:
As many as 67 Nepali citizens have died in Japan over the past ten months, including 25 suicides, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Most of the deceased were individuals who had travelled on student visas and were also working part-time.

The deaths were recorded between mid-July, 2025 and June 1, 2026. While some cases list medical or other causes, many certificates state the reason as “unknown”. Illness-related deaths remain relatively low, officials said.

Acting Nepali ambassador to Japan Harihar Kant Poudel said the rising number of deaths has made body management increasingly difficult. “In some cases, families perform the funeral rites in Japan. In others, the embassy is not informed even after cremation,” he said.

Repatriating a body from Japan to Nepal costs around Rs1.2 million. Educational institutions sending students abroad on student visas are not covering these expenses and are often not in contact with the embassy.

Many students arriving for language studies on student visas have been taking up work. However, they are not required to obtain labour permits from the Department of Foreign Employment. As a result, the Foreign Employment Board does not provide financial assistance for repatriation or related support when deaths occur outside the formal labour system.

Deaths and suicides have been reported mainly among workers in construction, Nepal-run hotels and restaurants, and supply companies. Around 6,000 Nepal-operated hotels and restaurants are estimated to be running in Japan, where labour protections such as health insurance and social security are not consistently ensured.

Education consultancies in Nepal have been sending students to Japan by charging high fees and making what critics describe as misleading promises. Japanese government data shows that by 2025, around 116,000 Nepali students were living in Japan, making Nepal the second-largest source of foreign students after China. Overall, Nepalis are the fifth-largest migrant group in Japan, with a total population of about 309,000, including 9,908 permanent residents.

According to the Non-Resident Nepali Association Japan, many students are under severe financial and psychological pressure due to high-interest loans taken in Nepal.

“Living costs in Japan are high, and earnings from 28 working hours a week are not enough for rent, food and tuition,” said NRNA Japan secretary Sachin Acharya. “When families in Nepal demand loan repayments, it adds mental stress. Switching from student visas to work visas requires language proficiency and other conditions, which are difficult. This is contributing to rising suicides.”

He said many students come on student visas due to easier access, but struggle to find stable work. “Some have to rely on money from Nepal. Many Nepalis are being arrested for exceeding the 28-hour work limit,” he said. “The Nepali embassy is understaffed, which makes it difficult to handle prison visits and related cases.”

Nepali student Uma Khatri, currently in Japan, said the reality is far more difficult than expected. “You need strong Japanese language skills before coming here. It is manageable for those who can work hard, but very difficult for students,” she said. “City living is expensive. Rural areas are cheaper, but jobs are scarce. Attendance requirements are strict, and visa renewal can be affected.”

Hira Shrestha from Baglung, who paid Rs1.35 million to reach Japan, said even working beyond permitted hours does not ease financial pressure. “People expect to repay loans quickly, but many struggle for years,” he said. Survival itself is hard.”

He said consultancy firms often present an overly optimistic picture. “They say you can study language for a year and work, but there is no job guarantee. Competition for part-time work is intense,” he said. “Some take multiple jobs to save money, which is illegal and can lead to visa cancellation.”

Only a small number of Nepalis go to Japan as skilled workers, while many enter as trainees in the agriculture and business sectors. The Nepali embassy has urged authorities to avoid sending workers under individual labour permits through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and labour channels.

In the last fiscal year, 18,744 Nepalis received labour approval from the Department of Foreign Employment, including both institutional and individual permits, with 5,800 women among them.

The embassy said it mainly tracks trainee workers sent through approved channels, where employers or agencies can be held responsible in case of death, making repatriation easier. However, it lacks records of students and individuals who arrive outside formal labour approval systems, complicating assistance and monitoring.

articles.title: एभरेष्ट मार्ट स्टोरलाई दुई लाख जरिवाना
articles.summary:
स्थलगत अनुगमनका क्रममा कैफियत देखिएपछि वाणिज्य, आपूर्ति तथा उपभोक्ता संरक्षण विभागले काठमाडौं महानगरपालिका-१७ ठहिटीमा रहेको एभरेष्ट मार्ट स्टोर प्रालिलाई रु दुई लाखबराबरको जरिवाना गरेको छ।

अनुगमनका क्रममा तोकिएभन्दा बढी मूल्य लिएको पाइएपछि विभागले उपभोक्ता संरक्षण ऐन, २०७५ अनुसार कारबाही गरिएको जनाएको छ। यस्तै, गृष्मा इन्टरप्राइजेजलाई व्यवसायसँग सम्बन्धित कागजात लिई विभागमा उपस्थित हुन निर्देशन दिइएको छ।

यस्तै, सो फर्मलाई यही साउन १ गतेदेखि हालसम्मको खाना पकाउने ग्यासको बिक्री वितरणको विवरण, खरिद बिक्री बिलसमेत लिएर तीन दिनभित्र उपस्थित हुन भनिएको छ।

विभागले अन्य व्यावसायिक फर्मलाई भने सुधारात्मक निर्देशन दिएको छ। स्थानीय उपभोक्ता अधिकारकर्मी तथा सरोकारवालाको उपस्थितिमा विभागले नियमित रूपमा अनुगमन गर्दै आएको छ।

पछिल्ला दिनमा खाना पकाउने ग्यासमा देखिएको समस्या समाधानका लागि विभागले अनुगमन तथा निरीक्षणलाई थप प्रभावकारी बनाएको छ। अनुगमन तथा निरीक्षण गर्दा उपभोक्ता संरक्षण ऐन, २०७५ तथा उपभोक्ता संरक्षण नियमावली, २०७६ बमोजिम आवश्यक निर्देशक एवं कारबाही गरिएको जनाएको छ।

articles.title: आजका लागि तोकियो विदेशी मुद्राको विनिमयदर
articles.summary:
नेपाल राष्ट्र बैंकले आज (शुक्रबार) का लागि विदेशी मुद्राको विनिमयदर निर्धारण गरेको छ।

राष्ट्र बैंकका अनुसार अमेरिकी डलर एकको खरिददर १५२ रुपैयाँ ०६ पैसा र बिक्रीदर १५२ रुपैयाँ ६६ पैसा निर्धारण गरिएको छ।युरोपियन युरो एकको खरिददर १७५ रुपैयाँ ४५ पैसा र बिक्रीदर १७६ रुपैयाँ १४ पैसा, युके पाउन्ड स्ट्रलिङ एकको खरिददर २०४ रुपैयाँ ६२ पैसा र बिक्रीदर २०५ रुपैयाँ ४३ पैसा, स्वीस फ्र्याङ्क एकको खरिददर १८७ रुपैयाँ ८३ पैसा र बिक्रीदर १८८ रुपैयाँ ५७ पैसा कायम गरिएको छ।

अष्ट्रेलियन डलर एकको खरिददर १०७ रुपैयाँ ०८ पैसा र बिक्रीदर १०७ रुपैयाँ ५० पैसा, क्यानेडियन डलर एकको खरिददर १०८ रुपैयाँ ५३ पैसा र बिक्रीदर १०८ रुपैयाँ ९६ पैसा, सिङ्गापुर डलर एकको खरिददर ११८ रुपैयाँ ६० पैसा र बिक्रीदर ११९ रुपैयाँ ०७ पैसा तोकिएको छ।

जापानी येन १० को खरिददर नौ रुपैयाँ ६३ पैसा र बिक्रीदर नौ रुपैयाँ ६७ पैसा, चिनियाँ युआन एकको खरिददर २२ रुपैयाँ ५३ पैसा र बिक्रीदर २२ रुपैयाँ ६२ पैसा, साउदी अरेबियन रियाल एकको खरिददर ४० रुपैयाँ ४९ पैसा र बिक्रीदर ४० रुपैयाँ ६५ पैसा, कतारी रियाल एकको खरिददर ४१ रुपैयाँ ७१ पैसा र बिक्रीदर ४१ रुपैयाँ ८७ पैसा कायम भएको छ।

केन्द्रीय बैंकका अनुसार थाइ भाट एकको खरिददर चार रुपैयाँ ६० पैसा र बिक्रीदर चार रुपैयाँ ६२ पैसा, युएई दिराम एकको खरिददर ४१ रुपैयाँ ४० पैसा र बिक्रीदर ४१ रुपैयाँ ५७ पैसा, मलेसियन रिङ्गेट एकको खरिददर ३७ रुपैयाँ १८ पैसा र बिक्रीदर ३७ रुपैयाँ ३३ पैसा, साउथ कोरियन वन १०० को खरिददर १० रुपैयाँ ६७ पैसा र बिक्रीदर १० रुपैयाँ ७२ पैसा, स्वीडिस क्रोनर एकको खरिददर १६ रुपैयाँ ०५ पैसा र बिक्रीदर १६ रुपैयाँ ११ पैसा र डेनिस क्रोनर एकको खरिददर २३ रुपैयाँ ४७ पैसा र बिक्रीदर २३ रुपैयाँ ५६ पैसा तोकिएको छ।

राष्ट्र बैंकले हङकङ डलर एकको खरिददर १९ रुपैयाँ ३८ पैसा र बिक्रीदर १९ रुपैयाँ ४६ पैसा, कुवेती दिनार एकको खरिददर ४९५ रुपैयाँ १५ पैसा र बिक्रीदर ४९७ रुपैयाँ १० पैसा, बहराइन दिनार एकको खरिददर ४०३ रुपैयाँ २९ पैसा बिक्रीदर ४०४ रुपैयाँ ८८ पैसा, ओमनी रियाल एकको खरिददर ३९४ रुपैयाँ ९५ पैसा र बिक्रीदर ३९६ रुपैयाँ ५० पैसा रहेको छ।

भारतीय रुपैयाँ एक सयको खरिददर १६० रुपैयाँ र बिक्रीदर १६० रुपैयाँ १५ पैसा तोकेको छ । राष्ट्र बैंकले यो विनिमयदरलाई आवश्यकतानुसार जुनसुकै समयमा पनि संशोधन गर्न सकिने जनाएको छ । वाणिज्य बैंकले तोक्ने विनिमयदर भने फरक हुनसक्ने र अद्यावधिक विनिमयदर केन्द्रीय बैंकको ‘वेबसाइट’मा उपलब्ध हुने जनाइएको छ ।

articles.title: कक्षा १२ को मौका परीक्षामा ८१ प्रतिशतभन्दा बढी विद्यार्थी सफल
articles.summary:
राष्ट्रिय परीक्षा बोर्डले कक्षा १२ को मौका परीक्षाको नतिजा सार्वजनिक गरेको छ। बोर्डका अनुसार बिहीबार सार्वजनिक नतिजामा ७१ हजार ३१० परीक्षार्थी सहभागी भएका थिए।

तीमध्ये ५७ हजार ८९७ परीक्षार्थीले सबै विषयमा ग्रेड प्राप्त गरेका छन्। यो कुल परीक्षार्थीको ८१.१९ प्रतिशत हो। बोर्डले तीन परीक्षार्थीको परीक्षाफल भने रद्द गरेको जनाएको छ। नतिजामा प्राविधिक कारणले कुनै त्रुटि देखिएमा परीक्षा नियन्त्रण कार्यालयको मूल अभिलेखका आधारमा आवश्यक संशोधन गरिने बोर्डले जनाएको छ।

परीक्षार्थीले आफ्नो नतिजा बोर्डको वेबसाइट, एसएमएस तथा आइभीआर सेवामार्फत हेर्न सक्नेछन्। बोर्डले कक्षा १२ को मौका परीक्षा यही साउन २ र ३ गते सञ्चालन गरेको थियो ।

articles.title: वर्षाले सडक सञ्जाल प्रभावित, यात्रामा सावधानी अपनाउन अनुरोध
articles.summary:
वर्षाका कारण देशका विभिन्न जिल्लाका प्रमुख राजमार्ग तथा सडकखण्ड अवरुद्ध भएका छन्।

नेपाल प्रहरीले आज बिहान ५ः० बजेसम्मको विवरण सार्वजनिक गर्दै पहिरो, सडक कटान र सम्भावित बाढीका कारण एक दर्जनभन्दा बढी सडकखण्ड प्रभावित भएका जनाएको छ।

प्रहरीका अनुसार काभ्रेपलाञ्चोक–सिन्धुली जोड्ने बिपी राजमार्गमा सम्भावित बाढीको जोखिमलाई दृष्टिगत गर्दै खुर्कोट–नेपालथोक–कटुन्जेबेँसी सडकखण्डमा बेलुका ६ः०० देखि बिहान ४ः०० बजेसम्म सबै प्रकारका सवारीसाधन सञ्चालनमा रोक लगाइएको छ। बिहान ४ः०० देखि बेलुका ६ः०० बजेसम्म भने सवारी सञ्चालन हुने व्यवस्था मिलाइएको छ।

यसैगरी, कान्ति लोकपथमा पनि वर्षायामका कारण बेलुका ५ः०० देखि बिहान ५ः०० बजेसम्म सबै प्रकारका सवारीसाधन सञ्चालनमा रोक लगाइएको छ।

मेची राजमार्गअन्तर्गत इलाम नगरपालिका–९ राजदुवालीमा वर्षाका कारण सडक हिलाम्मे भएपछि यातायात पूर्ण रूपमा अवरुद्ध भएको छ। उक्त क्षेत्रमा वैकल्पिक मार्ग भने सञ्चालनमा छ।

सिन्धुपाल्चोकको भोटेकोशी गाउँपालिकाअन्तर्गत जिरोकिलो, कोदारी र लिपिङ क्षेत्रमा पहिरो र सडक भासिएपछि अरनिको राजमार्गका विभिन्न खण्ड पूर्ण रूपमा अवरुद्ध छन्।

लामासाँघु–रामेछाप सडकखण्डको दोलखाको तामाकोशी गाउँपालिका–५ किर्नेटारमा सामाकोशी खोलाले सडक कटान गरेपछि यातायात अवरुद्ध भएको छ। यद्यपि खिम्ती ग्रामीण विद्युत् सहकारी संस्थाको कार्यालय परिसर हुँदै वैकल्पिक मार्ग सञ्चालनमा ल्याइएको प्रहरीले जनाएको छ।

यसैगरी, रसुवाको पासाङ ल्हामु सडक, मुगुको नाग्म–गमगढी सडक, बागलुङको जैमिनी नगरपालिका–८ बेलबगरस्थित कालीगण्डकी करिडोर, रुकुम पश्चिमको रिजेगार्ड खोलास्थित भेरी करिडोर तथा मुस्ताङको थासाङ गाउँपालिका–४ कैकु खोलास्थित बेनी–जोमसोम सडकखण्ड पनि पहिरोका कारण पूर्ण रूपमा अवरुद्ध छन्।

म्याग्दीमा रघुगङ्गा गाउँपालिका–२ बैसेरी र अन्नपूर्ण गाउँपालिका–७ भिरकाटे क्षेत्रमा सडक बगाउँदा बेनी–जोमसोम सडकखण्डका दुई स्थानमा यातायात अवरुद्ध भएको छ।

गुल्मीको रुरुक्षेत्र गाउँपालिका–४ लेखस्थित मदन भण्डारी सडकखण्डमा सुक्खा पहिरो खसेपछि यातायात अवरुद्ध भएको प्रहरीले जनाएको छ।

प्रहरीले वर्षायाममा पहिरो, बाढी र सडक कटानको जोखिम कायमै रहेकाले यात्रा गर्नुअघि सम्बन्धित निकायबाट सडक अवस्थाबारे जानकारी लिएर मात्र यात्रा गर्न सर्वसाधारणलाई आग्रह गरेको छ।

articles.title: एभरेष्ट मार्ट स्टोरलाई दुई लाख जरिवाना
articles.summary:
स्थलगत अनुगमनका क्रममा कैफियत देखिएपछि वाणिज्य, आपूर्ति तथा उपभोक्ता संरक्षण विभागले काठमाडौं महानगरपालिका-१७ ठहिटीमा रहेको एभरेष्ट मार्ट स्टोर प्रालिलाई रु दुई लाखबराबरको जरिवाना गरेको छ।

अनुगमनका क्रममा तोकिएभन्दा बढी मूल्य लिएको पाइएपछि विभागले उपभोक्ता संरक्षण ऐन, २०७५ अनुसार कारबाही गरिएको जनाएको छ। यस्तै, गृष्मा इन्टरप्राइजेजलाई व्यवसायसँग सम्बन्धित कागजात लिई विभागमा उपस्थित हुन निर्देशन दिइएको छ।

यस्तै, सो फर्मलाई यही साउन १ गतेदेखि हालसम्मको खाना पकाउने ग्यासको बिक्री वितरणको विवरण, खरिद बिक्री बिलसमेत लिएर तीन दिनभित्र उपस्थित हुन भनिएको छ।

विभागले अन्य व्यावसायिक फर्मलाई भने सुधारात्मक निर्देशन दिएको छ। स्थानीय उपभोक्ता अधिकारकर्मी तथा सरोकारवालाको उपस्थितिमा विभागले नियमित रूपमा अनुगमन गर्दै आएको छ।

पछिल्ला दिनमा खाना पकाउने ग्यासमा देखिएको समस्या समाधानका लागि विभागले अनुगमन तथा निरीक्षणलाई थप प्रभावकारी बनाएको छ। अनुगमन तथा निरीक्षण गर्दा उपभोक्ता संरक्षण ऐन, २०७५ तथा उपभोक्ता संरक्षण नियमावली, २०७६ बमोजिम आवश्यक निर्देशक एवं कारबाही गरिएको जनाएको छ।

articles.title: भूपेन्द्रसहित बैंकका उच्च अधिकारीमाथि छानबिन शुरु
articles.summary:
काठमाडौं । स्मार्ट टेलिकमको अर्बौं मूल्य बराबरको पूर्वाधार बिक्री प्रकरणले नेपालको दूरसञ्चार क्षेत्रमा ल्याएको तरंगको पराकम्प अझै कम भएको छैन । लाइसेन्स रद्द भएपछि राज्यको स्वामित्वमा आउनुपर्ने सम्पत्ति चार अर्ब ६० करोड रुपैयाँमा बिक्री भएको विषय अहिले अनुसन्धानको केन्द्रमा छ ।

सीआईबीले पूर्वअध्यक्ष भूपेन्द्र भण्डारीसहित बैंकका उच्च अधिकारीमाथि छानबिन अघि बढाएको छ । नेपालको दूरसञ्चार क्षेत्र एउटा प्रश्नले अझै तरंगित छ । राज्यको स्वामित्वमा आउनुपर्ने स्मार्ट टेलिकमको अर्बौं रुपैयाँ बराबरको सम्पत्ति कसरी निजी हातमा पुग्यो ? यसको जवाफ अझै मिल्न सकेको छैन । नेपाल प्रहरीको केन्द्रीय अनुसन्धान ब्युरो अर्थात् सीआईबीले यही प्रकरणमा नेपाल दूरसञ्चार प्राधिकरणका पूर्वअध्यक्ष भूपेन्द्र भण्डारीलाई पक्राउ गरी अनुसन्धान अघि बढाइरहेको छ ।

काठमाडौं जिल्ला अदालतले भण्डारीमाथि थप अनुसन्धानका लागि प्रहरीलाई ६ दिनको म्याद दिएको छ । उनीमाथि ठगी, आपराधिक विश्वासघात र संगठित अपराधसम्बन्धी कसुरमा अनुसन्धान भइरहेको छ ।

स्मार्ट टेलिकमले २०७० सालमा आधारभूत टेलिफोन सेवा सञ्चालनको अनुमति पाएको थियो । तर कम्पनीले नवीकरण दस्तुर र रोयल्टीबापतको करिब ३० अर्ब रुपैयाँ सरकारलाई बुझाउन सकेन । त्यसपछि २०८० वैशाख ३ गते यसको लाइसेन्स स्वतः रद्द भयो ।

कानुनअनुसार लाइसेन्स रद्द भएको दूरसञ्चार कम्पनीको टावर, नेटवर्क, उपकरण र अन्य पूर्वाधार राज्यको स्वामित्वमा आउनुपर्ने व्यवस्था छ । तर सीआईबीको आरोप छः राज्यको नाममा आइसकेको स्मार्ट टेलिकमको सम्पत्ति नेपाल इन्भेष्टमेन्ट मेगा बैंकले गैरकानुनी रूपमा लिलामी ग¥यो र त्यो सम्पत्ति एनसेल आजियाटा लिमिटेडले खरिद ग¥यो । स्मार्टको लिलामी मूल्य थियो चार अर्ब ६० करोड रुपैयाँ ।

सीआईबीका अनुसार यो प्रक्रियामा तत्कालीन दूरसञ्चार प्राधिकरण अध्यक्ष भूपेन्द्र भण्डारीको भूमिका सबैभन्दा बढि शंकास्पद देखिएको छ । यही अनुसन्धानका क्रममा नेपाल इन्भेष्टमेन्ट मेगा बैंकका अध्यक्ष पृथ्वीबहादुर पाण्डेसहित ६ जना सञ्चालकको बैंक खाता रोक्का गरिएको छ । प्रहरीले उनीहरूविरुद्ध पक्राउ पुर्जीसमेत लिएको बताइएको छ ।

खाता रोक्का भएका व्यक्तिमा अध्यक्ष पाण्डेसँगै प्रणय राजभण्डारी, दीपांकर शाक्य, कविकुमार तिव्रेवाला, शालिकराम बेलवासे र शोभा श्रेष्ठ रहेका छन् ।

अर्का सञ्चालक मदनकुमार आचार्यले भने सीआईबीमा उपस्थित भएर बयान दिइसकेका कारण पक्राउ पुर्जीबाट बाहिर रहेको बुझिएको छ ।

फेरि एकपटक बिक्रि प्रक्रियाको कुरा गरौँ

स्मार्ट टेलिकमकोे सम्पत्ति बिक्री प्रक्रिया नेपाल इन्भेष्टमेन्ट मेगा बैंकले स्मार्ट टेलिकमले सम्पत्ति बिक्रिका लागि बोलपत्र आह्वान गरेसँगै अघि बढेको थियो । यसमा तीन कम्पनी सहभागी भए । ट्रान्सगेट टेकले ४४ करोड ५० लाख रुपैयाँ, प्रोफेसनल बिजनेस नेटवर्कले ४२ करोड ५० लाख रुपैयाँ र एनसेल आजियाटाले चार अर्ब ६० करोड रुपैयाँको प्रस्ताव पेस ग¥यो ।

बैंकले सबैभन्दा बढी रकम प्रस्ताव गर्ने एनसेलको बोलपत्र स्वीकार ग¥यो । तर यी तीन कम्पनीले राखेको खरिद मूल्य प्रस्ताव नै शंकास्पद देखिन्छ । सेटिङमै तीन कम्पनी एकै व्यक्तिबाट परिचालित देखिन्छ । दुई कम्पनीको प्रस्तावभन्दा एनसेल आजियाटाको प्रस्ताव आकाश जमिन फरक छ ।

यो किनबेचमा बैंकको दाबी छ, उसले ऋण असुलीका लागि बैंक तथा वित्तीय संस्थासम्बन्धी ऐनको व्यवस्थाअनुसार धितो बिक्री गरेको हो । तर जुन सम्पत्ति राज्यको स्वामित्वमा आइसकेको थियो, त्यसलाई बैंकले बिक्री गर्ने अधिकार कसरी पायो भन्ने सीआईबीको प्रश्न छ ।

यसअघि सीआईबीले स्मार्ट टेलिकमका सञ्चालक सर्वेश जोशी र नेपाल इन्भेष्टमेन्ट मेगा बैंकका प्रमुख कार्यकारी अधिकृत ज्योति प्रकाश पाण्डेलाई पनि पक्राउ गरी अनुसन्धान गरेको थियो । सीआईबीले केही महिनादेखि यो प्रकरणमाथि अध्ययन अनुसन्धान गरिरहेको छ ।

तत्कालिन मन्त्री शर्माको भूमिका !

भूपेन्द्र भण्डारी दूरसञ्चार प्राधिकरणको अध्यक्ष बन्नुअघि तत्कालिन सञ्चारमन्त्री रेखा शर्माका सल्लाहकार थिए । शर्माको जोडबलमा भण्डारीलाई प्राधिकरणको अध्यक्षमा तत्कालीन प्रधानमन्त्री पुष्पकमल दाहाल ‘प्रचण्ड’ नेतृत्वको सरकारले नियुक्त गरेको थियो । प्राधिकरण अध्यक्ष बन्नुअघि भण्डारी इन्टरग्रुप टेलिकम एसएल लिमिटेड र स्मार्ट मोबाइल बुरुन्डीको प्रमुख कार्यकारी अधिकृत भइसकेका व्यक्ति हुन् ।

उनले मरु डिजिटल वालेट चलाउने कम्पनी पेनेपमा अध्यक्षका रुपमा ५ वर्ष १० महिना काम गरेका थिए । कार्यकाल ७ महिना बाँकी छँदै प्राधिकरणका तत्कालीन अध्यक्ष पुरुषोत्तम खनालले तत्कालीन प्रधानमन्त्री प्रचण्ड र तत्कालीन सञ्चारमन्त्री शर्माको दबाब खेप्न नसकेपछि २०८० पुस २४ गते राजीनामा दिएपछि भण्डारी दूरसञ्चार क्षेत्रको नियामक प्राधिकरणको अध्यक्ष नियुक्त भएका थिए ।

वर्तमान सरकारले सार्वजनिक पदाधिकारीसम्बन्धी विशेष व्यवस्थाअन्तर्गत भण्डारीलाई पदबाट बर्खास्त गरेको हो । आलोचकहरूले भण्डारीको कार्यकालमा दूरसञ्चार क्षेत्रका समस्या थप बढेको आरोप लगाएका छन् । स्मार्ट टेलिकमका टावर राख्न दिएका दुई सयभन्दा बढी घरधनीले समेत लामो समयदेखि भाडा नपाएको गुनासो गर्दै आएका छन् ।

सीआईबीको अनुसन्धानले राज्यको स्वामित्वमा आउनु पर्ने अर्बौ मूल्यको दूरसञ्चार पूर्वाधार कानूनी प्रक्रियाबाट बिक्रि भएको थियो कि मिलेमतोमा भन्ने प्रश्नको उत्तर खोजिरहेको छ । स्मार्ट टेलिकम प्रकरणको अन्तिम निष्कर्ष अनुसन्धान र अदालतको प्रक्रियाले तय गर्नेछ ।

articles.title: टुसा व्यापारमा कडाई, पोखरामा माग भन्दा कम आपूर्ति
articles.summary:
कास्की । साउन लागेसँगै पोखराको बजारमा पहाडी क्षेत्रमा पाइने औषधीय गुणयुक्त टुसाको कारोबार सुरु भएको छ । पोखरा घुम्न आउने पर्यटकका लागि टुसा लोकप्रिय कोसेली बन्दै गए पनि यस वर्ष उत्पादन र आपूर्ति घट्दा व्यापार पनि सुस्त बनेको छ ।

अन्नपूर्ण संरक्षण क्षेत्र आयोजनाले चोरी निकासी नियन्त्रण गरेसँगै बजारमा टुसाको उपलब्धता कम भएको जनाएको छ । पोखरा घुम्न आउने धेरैजसो आन्तरिक पर्यटक फर्किने बेला स्थानीय कोसेलीका रूपमा टुसा लैजान रुचाउँछन् ।

औषधीय गुणले भरिपूर्ण मानिने टुसाको तरकारी पछिल्ला वर्षहरूमा झन् लोकप्रिय बन्दै गएको छ । अधिकांश टुसा पाइने क्षेत्र अन्नपूर्ण संरक्षण क्षेत्र आयोजना (एक्याप) अन्तर्गत पर्छन् । संरक्षणसँगै स्थानीयको आयआर्जनलाई समेत ध्यानमा राख्दै एक्यापले हरेक वर्ष साउन महिनाभर सर्वसाधारणलाई टुसा संकलन गर्न अनुमति दिने गरेको छ ।

असारदेखि भदौसम्म टुसा पलाउने मुख्य याम हो । कास्कीका ल्वाङ, घलेल, भुर्जुङखोला, सिक्लेस, ताङतिङ, याङजाकोट, घान्द्रुक, लान्द्रुक, धम्पुस र लुम्लेलगायत उच्च पहाडी क्षेत्रबाट बजारमा टुसा ल्याइन्छ । मानव स्वास्थ्यका लागि उपयोगी भएकाले यसको महत्व हरेक वर्ष बढ्दै गएको एक्यापको भनाइ छ ।

साउन महिनामा धेरैले माछामासु कम खाने परम्परा र यही समयमा टुसाको उत्पादन बढी हुने भएकाले व्यापार पनि बढ्ने गरेको थियो । तर यस वर्ष भने बजारको अवस्था फरक देखिएको छ । व्यापारीका अनुसार उत्पादन कम भएकाले बजारमा टुसाको आपूर्ति घटेको छ ।

अहिले पोखरामा प्रतिमुठा ८० देखि १५० रुपैयाँसम्ममा बिक्री भइरहेको छ । राम्रो व्यापार भएका दिन एकै स्थानबाट दुई सय मुठासम्म बिक्री हुने गरे पनि अघिल्लो वर्षको तुलनामा यसपालि कारोबार घटेको व्यवसायीको भनाइ छ ।

पछिल्ला वर्षहरूमा टुसाको चोरी निकासी बढेपछि एक्यापले व्यवस्थापन कडा बनाएको छ । बोलकबोल प्रक्रियामार्फत वैधानिक रूपमा संकलन र बिक्रीको व्यवस्था गरिएको छ ।

अघिल्ला वर्षमा करिब ९ लाख टुसा निकासा गरिएकोमा यस वर्ष ६ लाख मात्रै निकासा गरिएको र चोरी निकासी नियन्त्रण गरिएकाले पनि बजारमा टुसाको उपलब्धता कम भएको एक्यापले जनाएको छ ।

उच्च पहाडी क्षेत्रको प्राकृतिक उत्पादन टुसा जडीबुटी मात्र होइन, पोखराको पहिचान बनेको कोसेली पनि हो । तर उत्पादनमा कमी र अवैध निकासी नियन्त्रणको प्रभाव यस वर्ष बजारमा स्पष्ट देखिएको छ ।

संरक्षण र व्यवस्थित व्यवस्थापनसँगै उत्पादन बढाउन सकिए टुसाको व्यापारले स्थानीय अर्थतन्त्रलाई अझ बलियो बनाउने अपेक्षा समेत गरिएको छ ।

articles.title: महारथीको सम्मान लिन नेपाल आउँदै जनरल सेठ
articles.summary:
काठमाडौं । नेपाल–भारत सैनिक सम्बन्धको पुरानो परम्परालाई निरन्तरता दिन भारतीय स्थल सेनाप्रमुख जनरल धीरज सेठ साउन ३१ गते नेपाल भ्रमणमा आउँदैछन् । मानार्थ महारथीको सम्मान पाउने जनरल सेठको यो भ्रमणसँगै गोर्खा भर्ती, अग्निपथ योजना र सीमामा नेपाली नागरिकमाथि हुने व्यवहारका विषय पनि चर्चामा छन् ।

भारतीय स्थल सेनाका प्रमुख जनरल धीरज सेठ पाँच दिने औपचारिक भ्रमणका लागि साउन ३१ गते अर्थात् अगस्ट १६ मा नेपाल आउँदैछन् । नेपाली सेनाका प्रधानसेनापति अशोकराज सिग्देलको निमन्त्रणामा हुन लागेको यो भ्रमणलाई नेपाल–भारत सैनिक सम्बन्धको निरन्तरताका रूपमा हेरिएको छ ।

भ्रमणका क्रममा जनरल सेठलाई नेपाली सेनाको मानार्थ महारथी दर्जाको दज्र्यानी चिह्न प्रदान गरिने कार्यक्रम छ । सन् १९५० देखि नेपाल र भारतले एकअर्काका सेना प्रमुखलाई मानार्थ महारथीको सम्मान प्रदान गर्दै आएका छन् । यो परम्परालाई दुई देशबीचको विश्वास, मित्रता र सैनिक सहकार्यको एउटा विशिष्ट प्रतिक मानिएको छ ।

यसअघि २०८१ मंसिर २७ गते नेपाली सेनाका प्रधानसेनापति अशोकराज सिग्देललाई भारतको नयाँदिल्लीमा आयोजित विशेष समारोहमा भारतीय राष्ट्रपति द्रौपदी मुर्मुले भारतीय सेनाको मानार्थ महारथीको दज्र्यानी चिह्न प्रदान गरेकी थिइन् ।

नेपाल–भारत सैनिक सम्बन्ध !

नेपाल र भारतबीचको सैनिक सम्बन्ध शताब्दीयौँ पुरानो मानिन्छ । स्वतन्त्र भारत र नेपालबीच सन् १९५० को शान्ति तथा मैत्री सन्धिपछि दुई देशबीचको रक्षा सहकार्य अझ संस्थागत बनेको हो । दुवै देशका सेनाले संयुक्त सैन्य अभ्यास सूर्य किरण, विपद् व्यवस्थापन, सीमा सुरक्षासम्बन्धी समन्वय, तालिम आदान–प्रदान तथा उच्च तहका भ्रमणलाई निरन्तरता दिँदै आएका छन् ।

यस्तै नेपाली नागरिक भारतीय सेनामा भर्ती हुने व्यवस्था पनि दुई देशबीचको विशेष सम्बन्धको अर्को आधार हो ।

गोर्खा सैनिकका रूपमा नेपाली युवाले करिब दुई सय वर्षदेखि भारतीय सेनामा सेवा गर्दै आएका छन् । अहिले पनि हजारौँ नेपाली नागरिक भारतीय सेनाका विभिन्न गोर्खा रेजिमेन्टमा कार्यरत छन् भने ठूलो संख्यामा पूर्वगोर्खा सैनिकले पेन्सन र अन्य सुविधा प्राप्त गरिरहेका छन् ।

अग्निपथले रोकिएको भर्ति !

तर पछिल्ला वर्षमा भारतीय सेनाको अग्निपथ योजना लागू भएपछि नेपाली नागरिकको भर्ती प्रक्रिया प्रभावित भएको छ । नेपाल सरकारले अग्निपथ योजनाबारे औपचारिक धारणा नटुंग्याएको भन्दै नेपाली युवाको भारतीय सेनामा नयाँ भर्ती रोकिएको अवस्था छ ।

चार वर्षे कार्यकाल र त्यसपछि २५ प्रतिशतलाई मात्रै नियमित सेवामा राखिने अग्गिपथ अन्तर्गतको मापदण्डका कारण लामो समयदेखि कायम रहेको गोर्खा भर्ती रोकिएको हो । यो विषयमा दुवै देशबीच कूटनीतिक तहमा छलफल हुँदै आएको छ ।

सीमा दुखेको सम्बन्ध !

नेपाली सेना र भारतीय सेनाबीच मानार्थ महारथीको विशिष्ट परम्परा रहँदा रहँदै पनि सीमामा भारतीय सीमा सुरक्षा बल एसएसबीले नेपाली नागरिकमाथि गर्ने दुव्र्यवहारका घटना बेलाबेला सार्वजनिक हुँदै आएका छन् ।

एसएसबीले सीमा क्षेत्रमा कुटपिट, अनावश्यक नियन्त्रण, गोली चलाइएका घटना तथा नेपाली नागरिकमाथि भएको दुव्र्यवहारले नेपाली नागरिकले अक्सर भारतसँग चित्त दुखाउनु परेको छ । यस्ता घटनापछि नेपाली पक्षबाट कूटनीतिक विरोध भएपनि दीर्घकालीन समाधान भने हुन सकेको छैन ।

articles.title: वित्तीय क्षेत्रको निष्पक्षता नै अर्थतन्त्रको मेरुदण्डः एक्यान अध्यक्ष नेपाल
articles.summary:
काठमाडौं । नेपाल चार्टर्ड एकाउण्टेण्ट्स संघ (एक्यान) का अध्यक्ष अनुप नेपालले वित्तीय क्षेत्रको निष्पक्षता नै अर्थतन्त्रको मेरुदण्ड भएको बताएका छन् ।

नेपाल अडिटर्स एसोसिएसन (अडान) को वार्षिक साधारण सभालाई सम्बोधन गर्दै उनले मुलुकको अर्थतन्त्रमा पारदर्शिता र वित्तीय सुशासन कायम गर्न लेखापरीक्षण क्षेत्रको भूमिका महत्वपूर्ण हुने बताए । उनले राज्यको राजस्व सङ्कलनलाई पारदर्शी बनाउन र व्यावसायिक क्षेत्रमा विश्वास अभिवृद्धि गर्न लेखापरीक्षकहरूले गरेको योगदानको प्रशंसा गरे ।

एक्यान र अडान दुवै संस्थाको साझा लक्ष्य नेपाली लेखा व्यवसायलाई थप मर्यादित, पारदर्शी र उत्तरदायी बनाउनु रहेको भन्दै उनले पेसागत हकहित र नीतिगत सुधारका लागि सहकार्य आवश्यक रहेको बताए ।

उनले आजको समय प्रविधिमैत्री युग रहेको भन्दै यसमा पनि अडिटर्सहरुले आफूलाई प्रविधिमैत्री बनाउनुपर्नेमा जोड दिए । अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय लेखापरीक्षण मापदण्ड र कर प्रणालीका नयाँ चुनौतीहरूको सामना गर्नका दक्षता अभिवृद्धि गर्नुपर्ने उनको सुझाव छ । पछिल्लो समयको एआई प्रविधिहरुबाट कोही पनि आतंकित हुनु नपर्ने भन्दै प्रविधिलाई केवल एउटा साधनका रूपमा लिन उनले आग्रह गरे ।

उनले क्याल्कुलेटरको आविष्कारको उदाहरण दिँदै क्याकुलेटर आज सामान्य र आवश्यक भएजस्तै एआई जस्ता प्रविधिहरु आगामी दशकमा उस्तै अत्यावश्यक बन्ने बताए ।

खासगरी उच्च व्यावसायिक नैतिकता, निष्पक्षता र इमानदारितालाई आत्मसाथ गरि समाज र राज्यको लेखापरीक्षण पेशाप्रतिको विश्वासलाई मजबुत बनाउनुपर्नेमा उनले जोड दिएका छन् ।

articles.title: Teen’s fatal shooting in Siraha still a mystery as forensic probe begins
articles.summary:
The mystery surrounding the fatal shooting of a 15-year-old boy during unrest in Siraha has deepened after Nepal’s three security agencies denied firing the bullet that killed him, prompting authorities to expand the investigation with ballistic and forensic experts.

Ganesh Yadav, a resident of ward 2 in Aurahi Rural Municipality, was shot in the neck during violence in Golbazar on July 30, four days after communal tensions triggered by a clash between two communities in Dewanganj of Sunsari spread across Madhesh Province.

His body remained in Golbazar Chowk for nearly three hours as grieving relatives demanded answers. A video showing his elder brother, Kamlesh Yadav, aged 18, breaking down while informing relatives about the shooting quickly went viral, adding to public anger and fuelling tensions.

Home Minister Sudan Gurung travelled to Madhesh Province shortly after the incident and met Ganesh’s father Ram Briksh Yadav in Siraha. The family agreed to collect the body only after signing a seven-point agreement with the government. Yet the central question remains: whose bullet killed the teenager?

Chief District Officer Surendra Paudel of Siraha said that local authorities had been briefed that Nepal Police personnel fired only blank rounds and rubber bullets in their efforts to control the situation. “We have also been informed that the Armed Police Force did not fire live ammunition,” Paudel told Kantipur.

Deputy Inspector General Abi Narayan Kafle, the Nepal Police spokesperson, said the Madhesh Province Police Office had formed an investigation committee led by Superintendent Bhesh Raj Rijal on the day of the incident. He added that the home ministry had also constituted a separate committee to examine the broader circumstances surrounding the unrest.

A curfew had been imposed in Golbazar as violence escalated, and Nepali Army personnel were also deployed to assist civil authorities. However, the army has likewise denied firing live ammunition. Nepali Army spokesperson Brigadier General Rajaram Basnet said he could not comment on the issue because it was under investigation.

The home ministry-formed committee, led by Joint Secretary Pushparaj Shahi, has also yet to determine who fired the fatal shot. A member of the panel said identifying the source of the bullet had become one of the most challenging aspects of the inquiry.

“The question of who fired the bullet has been more complicated than it initially appeared, and we are treating it as our top priority,” the committee member told Kantipur.

As uncertainty persisted, the ministry expanded the investigation team by adding two officials from the Nepal Police Forensic Science Laboratory to conduct detailed ballistic and forensic examinations, raising hopes that scientific analysis will establish responsibility for the teenager’s death.

The newly added investigators are Inspector Dipesh Awasthi and Superintendent of Police Manohar Singh Dhami, who specialise in ballistic and forensic analysis. They joined an existing panel comprising Nepal Police Superintendent Mohan Kumar Thapa, Armed Police Force Superintendent Naresh Bhandari, Central Police Forensic Science Laboratory Deputy Superintendent Pawan Kumar Dhungana, and Home Ministry Under Secretary Kul Shekhar Aryal.

A home ministry official said the team was strengthened because scientific evidence was considered essential to determine which weapon fired the fatal shot. Ballistic testing can identify the firearm used and estimate the firing distance, findings investigators believe will help reconstruct the sequence of events.

Buddha Narayan Sahani, head of the National Human Rights Commission’s Madhesh office, said that there was still no confirmed answer despite widespread speculation. “Many claims have been made, but nothing has been conclusively established,” he told Kantipur, adding that the commission was conducting its own assessment.

According to security officials, similar incidents in the past have also been marked by uncertainty over which party fired the fatal shot.

Former Additional Inspector General of Nepal Police Uttam Raj Subedi said uncertainty over responsibility was not unprecedented in crowd-control operations involving multiple security agencies.

“Ballistic examination can determine which weapon fired the bullet,” he said. “Once investigators establish which personnel were deployed and which weapons they carried, identifying responsibility should not be difficult.”

Subedi added that investigators must also consider the possibility that someone outside the security forces fired the shot if no agency accepts responsibility.

Ganesh’s father, Ram Briksh Yadav, has consistently maintained that the government is responsible for his son’s death. “The government killed my child. Whoever fired the bullet must be punished. I want justice,” he said. He repeated the same demand when Home Minister Gurung visited his home on July 31.

Under the second point of agreement signed by Gurung, the government committed to an impartial and effective investigation into the Golbazar incident and immediate legal action against those found responsible.

Accordingly, the Shahi-led team began its inquiry. After arriving in Siraha, the committee started inspecting the incident site, collecting evidence and other relevant facts, and holding consultations with local residents and other stakeholders.

Investigators also held an all-party meeting at Golbazar Municipality, met business owners to document losses caused during the unrest, and separately consulted representatives of the Muslim community on the causes of the violence and ways to restore social harmony.

The committee is also examining whether security personnel followed established procedures governing the use of force. International human rights standards require lethal force to be used only as a last resort, while Nepal’s Local Administration Act allows live ammunition only under exceptional circumstances after clear warnings are issued. Residents have alleged that no such warning was given.

The Siraha shooting came only days after police firing during communal violence in Sunsari’s Dewanganj left several people dead and injured, renewing concerns over the use of lethal force during crowd control.

According to the Local Government Act 1972, security personnel may resort to live fire only as a last resort when law and order cannot be maintained by any other means. Before opening fire, authorities are required to give a clear warning to the crowd. International crowd-control principles likewise require security forces to exercise restraint and use the minimum force necessary to bring a situation under control.

Local residents, however, say no warning was issued before shots were fired. Clause 6(B) of the Local Government Act states that if a crowd refuses to disperse and firing becomes unavoidable, a written and signed order must be issued, and shots should be aimed below the knees.

However, most of those injured in the Sunsari incident received gunshots above the knees. Ganesh was shot in the neck. His post-mortem examination was conducted at the BP Koirala Institute of Health Sciences in Dharan, and the hospital says the report has already been prepared.

articles.title: Inside Gandaki’s new cannabis law: Who can grow it, where, and under what rules
articles.summary:
Gandaki Province has formally opened the door to the cultivation of cannabis for medicinal and industrial use after its province chief authenticated a landmark law that establishes one of the country’s most comprehensive regulatory regimes for the crop.

The Bill to Regulate and Utilise Cannabis Cultivation for Medicinal and Industrial Purposes, 2026 was authenticated on Monday by Gandaki Chief Dilliraj Bhatta after surviving a constitutional dispute over whether the province had exceeded its legislative authority.

Once published in the provincial gazette, the law will come into force, although detailed regulations and implementation guidelines still need to be drafted before cultivation licences can be issued.

The legislation aims to create employment and generate income by allowing commercial cannabis cultivation on suitable land while keeping production under strict government control. Rather than legalising cannabis for general use, the law establishes a tightly regulated licensing system limited to medicinal and industrial purposes, with criminal penalties for violations.

A narrow legal opening

The Act carefully distinguishes between cannabis as a narcotic and cannabis-derived materials intended for industrial or pharmaceutical use.

Under the law, “cannabis” includes the leaves, flowers, seeds and fruit of the cannabis plant, along with naturally occurring resin and extracts. However, materials such as stalks, fibre, bark, roots, seeds, leaves and flowers intended as industrial raw materials or pharmaceutical ingredients are classified separately as “cannabis-derived products.”

That distinction is central to the legislation because it separates parts of the plant that could be used as narcotics from those intended for manufacturing medicines, fibre, textiles, oils and other industrial products.

The law defines medicinal use as cannabis supplied to pharmaceutical manufacturers registered with Nepal’s Department of Drug Administration or produced under the recommendation of licensed medical practitioners. Industrial use includes the manufacture of fibre, seed products, oils, textiles and other industrial raw materials.

Cultivation restricted to designated zones

Cannabis cultivation will not be permitted across the province.

Instead, Gandaki’s Ministry of Industry and Tourism will designate specific cultivation zones after receiving recommendations from a newly created Cannabis Cultivation Regulation and Management Unit.

Only selected districts or local units notified in the provincial gazette will be eligible for cultivation.

Authorities must consider land suitability, production potential, crop quality, public security, ease of monitoring and the impact on food production before approving cultivation areas. The law also instructs the government to prioritise barren, fallow or low-productivity land wherever possible.

The ministry must consult local units before declaring cultivation zones and will also determine the maximum area each licence holder may cultivate. The provincial government may later increase or reduce those limits based on recommendations from regulators.

THC capped at 0.3%

One of the law's most significant safeguards is a limit on the concentration of tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the principal psychoactive compound in cannabis.

Before harvesting, storage, transportation, processing or sale, cannabis must contain no more than 0.3% THC, the internationally recognised threshold commonly used to distinguish industrial hemp from psychoactive cannabis.

The province may establish its own testing laboratories or partner with universities and research institutions to analyse THC levels before products enter the market.

Three-stage licensing process

The law creates a three-tier approval system intended to prevent speculative licensing and ensure only qualified applicants enter the sector.

The first stage requires prospective growers to obtain preliminary approval.

Applicants must submit detailed information including proof of land ownership or lease agreements, recommendations from the relevant local government, intended medicinal or industrial use, estimated production volumes and a purchase commitment from a pharmaceutical or manufacturing company willing to buy the harvest.

Authorities will refuse applications for plots smaller than two ropanis (about 1,018 square metres) or larger than the maximum size prescribed for a designated cultivation zone.

Preliminary approval remains valid for one year. Applicants who fail to complete the required infrastructure and obtain a cultivation licence within that period must begin the process again.

The second stage requires growers to construct mandatory infrastructure before receiving a licence.

This includes perimeter fencing or walls to prevent unauthorised access, security systems, processing facilities if on-site processing is planned, and secure storage facilities for harvested crops.

Only after those requirements have been completed may applicants proceed to the final licensing stage.

Applicants must then provide detailed land records, photographs of cultivation sites, lease agreements of at least five years where applicable, purchase agreements with authorised buyers, declarations confirming they have not been convicted of drug-related offences during the previous ten years, and confirmation that all required infrastructure has been completed.

Government inspectors will conduct on-site inspections before licences are issued.

Licences may authorise cultivation for medicinal use, industrial use or both.

Strict obligations after licensing

Obtaining a licence does not free growers from continuous government oversight.

Licence holders must maintain all approved security infrastructure and may use or sell cannabis only for the purposes specified in their permits.

Any theft, damage or loss of crops must immediately be reported to both police and the regulatory unit with supporting evidence.

Growers must notify regulators, police and local monitoring committees before harvesting, storing or selling any crop.

They must also maintain updated records detailing cultivated area, plant numbers, production volumes, sales and purchasers.

Cultivation licences will remain valid for five years and require renewal before expiry.

Authorities may revoke licences if growers violate the law, breach licence conditions, fail to renew permits, sell products without prior approval, neglect required security infrastructure or fail to maintain production records.

Licence holders are entitled to present their defence before cancellation, except where they voluntarily surrender their licences. Appeals may be lodged within 35 days, although the appellate authority's decision will be final.

Harvesting and transport under official supervision

The Act imposes unusually stringent controls over harvesting and transportation.

Growers must electronically notify regulators once crops mature.

A government inspector will schedule the harvest and must be physically present before cutting begins.

Harvest quantities must be formally documented in the presence of the ward chair or representative, members of the local monitoring committee and police officials. The record must then be submitted to the regulatory unit.

If inspectors fail to arrive and crops risk deterioration, growers may request permission from the local monitoring committee to proceed.

Transport is subject to even tighter controls.

Cannabis products may only be transported after inspectors seal every shipment and record its contents.

The sealed consignments cannot be opened during transit.

They may only be unsealed at the final destination in the presence of district administration officials and police.

If a vehicle breaks down or is involved in an accident, authorities must reseal the cargo and document the incident before transport can resume.

Where a contracted purchaser refuses to accept a shipment, growers may sell it to another authorised processor only with government approval.

Any parts of the cannabis plant deemed capable of being used as narcotics but unsuitable for industrial or medicinal purposes must be destroyed after harvest, with police and regulators receiving formal destruction reports.

Four-tier oversight structure

The legislation creates a multilayered regulatory system.

At the top sits a provincial steering committee chaired by the chief minister. Members include ministers responsible for agriculture, health, industry and forests, the principal secretary, the provincial police chief and senior bureaucrats.

The committee will identify cultivation zones, resolve policy issues, recommend taxation, oversee regulation and coordinate public awareness programmes against drug abuse.

Day-to-day regulation will be handled by the Cannabis Cultivation Regulation and Management Unit under the Ministry of Industry and Tourism.

The unit will be headed by a senior director and supported by inspectors responsible for licensing, monitoring and enforcement. If necessary, police officers may be seconded to assist inspections.

At the local level, ward chairs will head monitoring committees comprising police representatives, agricultural officials, civil society members, farmers' representatives and ward secretaries.

These committees will supervise cultivation sites and report violations.

Criminal penalties remain

The law does not decriminalise unauthorised cannabis cultivation.

Anyone cultivating cannabis without a licence, growing beyond the authorised area or selling products outside the approved system will remain liable under Nepal’s national narcotics laws.

Less serious administrative violations, such as failing to maintain records or transporting products without required approvals or official seals, carry fines ranging from Rs50,000 to Rs500,000.

Inspectors must immediately refer serious offences to relevant investigative authorities for criminal proceedings.

Cannabis purchased for medicinal or industrial purposes must be used exclusively for those approved purposes, with detailed records maintained throughout the supply chain.

The provincial government also retains the authority to prohibit cultivation of particular cannabis varieties if future research shows they pose unacceptable public health risks.

Income earned from licensed cultivation will be treated as agricultural income for taxation purposes. Foreign investment and exports, however, will continue to be governed by existing federal laws.

Rehabilitation provisions

Recognising concerns over potential misuse, the law also provides for rehabilitation centres to treat cannabis addiction and substance abuse.

The centres may be established and operated by provincial or local governments, either independently or in partnership with communities and non-governmental organisations.

Constitutional dispute

The legislation reached the statute book only after an unprecedented constitutional confrontation between the provincial assembly and the province chief.

The bill was first passed by the Gandaki Provincial Assembly on July 14 and forwarded to Bhatta for authentication.

Instead of signing it, Bhatta returned the bill to the assembly, arguing that several provisions potentially conflicted with federal legislation, particularly Nepal’s Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act, 1976, and questioning whether the province had legislated beyond its constitutional powers.

It was the first time in Gandaki Province’s history that a governor had returned a bill for reconsideration.

The provincial assembly, however, rejected the governor'’s concerns and, after a brief debate, passed the bill again without making a single amendment.

Provincial ministers and lawmakers argued that agriculture falls within the exclusive legislative authority of provincial governments under Nepal’s Constitution and that older unitary-era legal provisions inconsistent with the federal constitution had already become inoperative.
