Under Article 201(4) of the Constitution, once a provincial assembly passes a bill for a second time, with or without amendments, the governor is constitutionally required to authenticate it within 15 days.

Bhatta subsequently signed the legislation three days after receiving it for the second time.

Province says law does not conflict with federal legislation

Gandaki’s Chief Attorney, Chiranjeevi Sharma Paudel, has defended the Act as fully consistent with both the Constitution and Nepal’s existing legal framework.

Paudel argues that Nepal never entirely closed the legal door to cannabis cultivation.

Although Nepal banned cannabis cultivation under the Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act after joining the 1961 Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, he says the country entered reservations allowing cultivation and trade for medicinal and industrial purposes.

He also contends that Nepal’s narcotics law itself permits the government to authorise controlled cultivation under special licences and allows cannabis to be supplied for pharmaceutical production.

According to Paudel, agriculture is an exclusive provincial subject under Schedule 6 of Nepal’s Constitution, giving Gandaki clear constitutional authority to legislate in this area.

He further argues that constitutional provisions rendered outdated sections of pre-federal legislation inoperative where they conflict with the federal constitutional order.

Paudel also notes that the World Health Organisation and the United Nations Commission on Narcotic Drugs have recognised the medicinal value of cannabis and revised its international classification, strengthening the case for regulated cultivation.

Even so, he acknowledges that the province’s success will depend on effective implementation, including strong licensing procedures, rigorous inspections and close coordination with local administrations.

“The law has been introduced primarily to benefit farmers,” he said, adding that practical difficulties could be addressed through future amendments.

Whether Gandaki’s model becomes a blueprint for other provinces, however, will largely depend on how effectively the government translates the law into functioning regulations and whether it can demonstrate that commercial cannabis cultivation can be managed without fuelling illicit production.

articles.title: Supreme Court reopens Nepali Congress leadership row
articles.summary:
The Supreme Court has reopened the legal dispute over the leadership of the Nepali Congress after deciding to review its earlier ruling that recognised the party’s special general convention and the central working committee led by Gagan Thapa.

A three-justice bench comprising Chief Justice Manoj Kumar Sharma and justices Nityananda Pandey and Shreekanta Paudel on Thursday issued the order while responding to separate review petitions filed by former party president Sher Bahadur Deuba and former acting president Purna Bahadur Khadka.

Both argued that the Supreme Court’s April verdict, which upheld the Election Commission’s recognition of Thapa’s leadership, was flawed.

The court’s order revives the dispute but does not immediately change the party’s leadership. The Election Commission’s decision recognising the Thapa-led central committee remains valid until the court issues a fresh ruling. As a result, Thapa continues to serve as party president and his central working committee retains legal authority.

Seeking to correct what they described as an “erroneous” Court ruling, Deuba and Khadka filed separate petitions for judicial review on July 22 and July 28, respectively.

The fresh order effectively resets the case to the stage before the April judgment.

A new three-justice bench, excluding the justices involved in the earlier verdict and Thursday’s review order, will hear the case from the beginning. The Supreme Court will notify all respondents, including the Election Commission and the Thapa-led leadership, seek written responses, obtain the commission’s original records and examine evidence submitted by both sides before delivering a final judgment.

The review comes as the Nepali Congress was edging closer to a formal split. Thapa, elected party president through the special general convention in January, now faces renewed pressure, while Deuba’s faction has been emboldened after the court’s decision. The faction had been preparing to form a separate party after concluding that efforts to bridge the divide within the party were unlikely to succeed.

Deuba’s faction had called a national gathering in Kathmandu for August 14 to 16 and had been preparing to launch a separate political party if unity efforts failed.

Former acting president Khadka had declined to lead the proposed new party, after which senior leaders persuaded Shashank Koirala, son of the party founder and ideologue BP Koirala, to head the organising committee and potentially assume its leadership. Accordingly, preparations were underway to present proposals on the party statute, finances, politics and contemporary political issues at the gathering scheduled to start on August 14.

Following Thursday’s order, however, leaders from the Deuba camp signalled a change in strategy. Leader Bimalendra Nidhi said the national gathering would proceed but that immediate plans to form a separate party would likely be dropped.

“There is no plan to postpone the gathering as of now. We will sit for discussions tomorrow [Friday]. Sher Bahadur ji is scheduled to return on August 11, and we will decide our next steps after consultations,” Nidhi told Kantipur. “The court’s order restores constitutionalism, and the rule of law is a historic step.”

Asked whether the gathering would move towards forming a separate party, Nidhi said, “We will no longer move towards forming a separate party. If the Supreme Court has granted a review, why would there be a need to create a separate party?”

Leaders aligned with Thapa also urged restraint. Vice-president Bishwa Prakash Sharma said that although the case had already been fully argued before the Supreme Court, the review would provide an opportunity to present the legal and political legitimacy of the special general convention in greater detail. He said his faction was prepared to present all relevant facts before the court.

“There was no need to reopen a matter for review after the Supreme Court’s joint bench had already settled it by quashing the writ petition following lengthy arguments,” he said. “However, I believe the review process will help shed further light on the legal facts and political realities surrounding the special general convention.”

General Secretary Pradip Paudel said the court’s decision to review the case should not be interpreted as a victory or defeat for either side. Instead, he argued that it had created an opportunity for broader party unity and urged leaders to seek a political settlement rather than waiting for the court’s final decision.

The ruling has also raised questions about the process for the party’s upcoming 15th general convention. The Congress is scheduled to begin ward-level conventions on August 18, followed by the national convention from September 30 to October 5. Party leaders said they would discuss whether the existing timetable should be maintained in light of the court proceedings.

In its order, the Supreme Court indicated that one of the principal legal issues requiring further examination is whether the Election Commission violated procedural fairness by recognising the new leadership without allowing the petitioners to present their case. The court referred to provisions of the Political Parties Act and Political Parties Regulations governing the updating of party records, suggesting that compliance with these procedural requirements needs scrutiny.

The dispute emerged after the Election Commission recognised the working committee elected under Thapa’s leadership at the special general convention. The Deuba faction challenged the commission’s decision at the Supreme Court.

On April 17, a division bench of Justices Sharanga Subedi and Nripdhwoj Niraula upheld the Election Commission’s decision to recognise the special general convention of the Congress as lawful. The ruling effectively validated the working committee elected from the convention and allowed the Thapa-led committee to continue carrying out party activities.

Legal experts said the review does not invalidate the earlier judgment or suspend the current leadership. Senior advocate and constitutional lawyer Purnaman Shakya said the Thapa-led leadership would remain in office until the court reached a final decision. He explained that the review simply reopens the legal examination and that the Supreme Court could ultimately either uphold or overturn its earlier ruling after considering fresh arguments and evidence.

Advocate Apurba Khatiwada said the legality of both the special general convention and the Election Commission’s decision would now be fully examined again, with the court reassessing the legal basis of the leadership change from the beginning.

In their review petitions, Deuba and Khadka set out 18 grounds challenging the earlier judgment. They argue that the Election Commission failed to conduct the inquiries required under the Political Parties Act before recognising the Thapa-led committee. They also contend that a special general convention cannot legally function as a regular general convention for electing a new central leadership.

The petition further argues that delegates had only demanded the convening of a special convention, not the election of new office-bearers, and that the then general secretary lacked both legal and moral authority to convene such a gathering. According to the petition, only the elected central working committee retained the authority to call a special convention under the party statute.

The Deuba faction also alleges that forged documents were submitted to the Election Commission, that signatures later withdrawn by delegates were ignored, and that the commission departed from procedures it had followed in previous disputes involving political parties. It further argues that an elected party president can only be removed through procedures laid down in the party statute and not through a special convention, while also questioning whether the convention had the number of delegates claimed by its organisers.

The dispute stems from the special general convention held from January 10 to 12, which elected Gagan Thapa and a new central working committee. The Election Commission recognised the new leadership on January 17, prompting Deuba and Khadka to challenge the decision in the Supreme Court.

Separately, Deuba is expected to return to Nepal on August 11 after nearly five months abroad. He spent some time in Singapore, where he has been “undergoing medical treatment” and later moved to Hong Kong. During his stay abroad, arrest warrants were issued against him and his wife, Arzu Rana Deuba, as part of a money laundering investigation.

Authorities sought an Interpol Red Notice, but the request was rejected. The Supreme Court has since issued an interim order preventing their arrest while it considers their legal challenge. Deuba had informed investigators that he was not absconding and would return to Nepal before mid-September to cooperate with the investigation.

articles.title: Nepal’s inclusion commissions are broke, powerless and mostly used as waiting rooms for politicians
articles.summary:
The 2015 Constitution of Nepal was touted as a transformative socio-economic document designed to rectify centuries of historical injustice against marginalised communities. A decade later, the seven inclusion commissions established through Part 27 of the Constitution to safeguard the rights of the marginalised stand as gaunt reminders of a promise unfulfilled. These institutions, born from the sweat and blood of the People’s Movement and the Tharuhat, Madhesh and Dalit struggles, have been reduced to ornamental fixtures within the state apparatus. As their ten-year review—mandated by Article 265 of the Constitution—looms, the state faces a difficult choice: Empower these commissions or admit that the inclusive project was merely an exercise in political window-dressing.

These commissions’ current state of ruin is a result of deliberate institutional starvation. The financial records of these bodies reveal a grotesque imbalance between administrative survival and community impact. In FY 2023-24, the Tharu Commission expended a total of Rs38.78 million, yet a pathetic Rs900,000 was allocated to programmes directly benefiting the community. Similarly, the Indigenous Nationalities Commission received Rs35.66 million for the FY 2024-25, with a mere Rs1.1 million designated for capital expenditure. When salaries and office rent consume 99 percent of each commission’s budget, they cease to be vehicles for social justice. Instead, they morph into taxpayer-funded waiting rooms for political appointees.

The powerlessness of these commissions is further calcified by a vacuum of legal authority and a wall of government indifference. Recommendations from these bodies are routinely treated as mere suggestions that the executive feels entitled to ignore. Of the 95 recommendations submitted by the Indigenous Nationalities Commission since its inception, only six have been implemented. The National Dalit Commission reports a similar trend, with less than 5 percent of its advice acted upon during a five-year tenure. While the Constitution explicitly defines the powers of the Women and Dalit commissions, it leaves the mandates of the Madhesi, Tharu and Muslim commissions to be determined by federal law, creating a hierarchy of rights that mocks the very principle of equality.

Over the years, the very integrity of these commissions has been eroded by political cronyism. Rather than appointing experts with proven records in research or advocacy, successive governments have used these constitutional seats as consolation prizes for loyalists who failed to secure election tickets. This degradation of meritocracy ensures that the commissions lack the teeth to challenge the status quo. Furthermore, the lack of permanent leadership—with the Tharu, Muslim and National Inclusion commissions currently languishing under acting officials—indicates a lack of state commitment to their success.

To argue that these bodies are redundant or burdensome would be to ignore the reality that electoral democracy alone cannot undo generations of systemic exclusion. A ministry focused on policy implementation will not independently audit its own failures. Constitutional commissions are essential. They serve as independent guarantors that protect rights on paper until they become rights in practice. Dissolving or merging these bodies into a single, diluted entity would be a retreat from the state’s obligation to provide specific institutional responses to distinct forms of historical discrimination.

The upcoming ten-year review must not be viewed as a constitutional death sentence but as an opportunity for institutional strengthening. Nepal requires a framework where commission recommendations carry legal weight, and the government is mandated to respond within a fixed timeframe. Financial autonomy of the commissions must be guaranteed to prevent the executive from using the budget as a leash to pull these bodies into submission. Ultimately, the credibility of Nepal’s democratic project rests on whether it views the marginalised as pillars of stability or as political inconveniences. True inclusion requires institutions with the resources, authority and independence to turn those words into practice.

articles.title: Electoral mandates alone cannot fix Nepal’s structural economic fragility
articles.summary:
Over the past 35 years, Nepal’s electoral landscape has produced four spectacular parliamentary mandates—won either by a single party or a unified alliance—including the most recent, a near two-thirds majority government led by Prime Minister Balendra Shah. Yet each of the three preceding majorities ultimately failed to complete its full five-year term, while coalition powers proved even more short-lived. Although intra-party disputes are the visible triggers for these government collapses, the root cause is subtle and systemic. In a country marked by both geographic and geopolitical vulnerabilities, a largely extractive political bureaucracy, and an economy that has persistently struggled to channel capital into productive capacity, the governing equilibrium remains fragile. Under such rigidity, even a dominant political power can quickly break down amid minor shocks, whether internal or external.

In April 2021, a government ban on synthetic fertilisers and agrochemicals severely harmed Sri Lanka’s agricultural market and food production, while exacerbating its foreign-exchange crisis, caused by pro-elite tax cuts, high debt-servicing costs and falling tourism revenue. With its ‘import-dependent for export’-type manufacturing model, which depends heavily on imported energy and intermediate goods, the country’s foreign reserves quickly dropped, and imports plummeted. The ripple effects brought Sri Lanka’s entire economic market, both domestic and international, to a standstill. The lack of a grip on markets and the consequent public frustration took no time to overthrow the Rajapaksa regime, despite its powerful two-thirds governing majority. The failure was not a shortage of capital or economic resources, but a persistent institutional inability to convert borrowing and financial inflows into productive capacity.

An abundance of money itself does not bring prosperity. Let’s imagine the economy as a big farm. If a large amount of money (received as remittances, for example) is spent repeatedly buying and selling the same plot of land at ever-increasing prices, money or assets change hands but grow no food; this is unproductive capital. Instead, money spent on a modern tractor, storage facilities, an upgraded irrigation system, or enhancing farmers’ technical skills represents productive capital.

Markets and powerholders

Markets are at the heart of economic prosperity. They allow people to take advantage of specialisation and division of labour, while enabling nations to expand trade based on comparative advantage. Since political markets seldom become efficient owing to the vagaries of representation, a nation’s long-run development and transformation require greater efficiency of economic markets.

Fundamentally, the size, flow and efficiency of investment capital are jointly determined by the interplay between government and markets. The better the state machinery facilitating the workings of the market, the greater the efficiency of resource allocation, including physical capital, human capital and natural resources. These two dynamic forces are inherently inseparable; consequently, a misstep in one inevitably damages the other. That’s why arrogance about a political majority amid structurally paralysed markets is a dangerous illusion for those in power.

Sovereign trade inequality

In a landlocked country like Nepal, where an ambulance essentially fuels up at the neighbour’s gas station, there is no such thing as ‘sovereign equality’ in market exchange. All countries are equal under the political framework of the Montevideo Convention of 1933, but not under the modern economic framework of the global village: cross-border trade relationships, transformative IT, financial innovation and digitalisation. A developing country’s trade and monetary policy independence is profoundly compromised when it pursues sustained gains on these fronts.

The economic giants, India and China, are not only neighbours, but also Nepal’s largest trading partners. Unfortunately, Nepal’s trade deficit with them is enormous; a recent report puts it at roughly $10 billion, or 77 percent of its overall trade deficit. If these figures raise serious concerns for policymakers, they must realise that borders are not simply geographical twists and turns; they hold extraordinary economic significance. Of course, borders matter, and neighbours matter. However, seeking diplomatic breakthroughs between neighbours matters even more.

Inward-looking impulse

Through persistent encroachment on domestic markets, Nepal’s ruling elites have stifled the cross-border integration necessary for harmonious bilateral trade with the country’s immediate neighbours. This intervention represents a systemic manifestation of political egoism, rather than a coherent economic strategy. The Panchayat regime’s import-substitution (IS) model kept the economy from harnessing the benefits of cross-border linkages at a time when globalisation was shaping the markets of developing nations.

The IS model was inherently inward-looking. It restricted cross-border transfers of cutting-edge technology, destroyed the spirit of innovation, discouraged entrepreneurs, and underestimated the rise of venture capital. Nepal’s isolation from broader regional and global value chains eroded the competitive edge needed for industrial productivity, leaving its manufacturing base in a state of persistent, structural decline. The aggressive liberalisation policies enacted during the democratic era merely exacerbated these structural vulnerabilities. By hiding behind the banner of sovereign equality, the Balendra Shah administration ignores the cross-border bilateral partnerships urgently needed to mobilise both internal and peripheral resources to revive manufacturing. Neighbourhood isolation and cross-border friction neither bring political stability nor generate economic gains.

Besides, the government’s credibility, or lack thereof, undeniably influences the incentives faced by private sector participants—either domestic or foreign. Consider an economic agenda set by the current administration: double the per capita income within five years. Based on the successful experiences of China and South Korea, doubling a country’s per capita income within five years requires an average annual real GDP growth rate of 14 percent or more, not 7 percent as targeted by the administration. While the target rate is already ambitious, this is an exceptionally large inconsistency. Furthermore, all other things being equal, the government also needs to proportionately double the allocation of capital expenditure from the customary 17 percent to 34 percent of the national budget, let alone the economy’s persistently meagre capacity to absorb it.

While taking to the streets for parliamentary democracy in 1990, many Nepalis sacrificed their lives with a simple hope of seeing a good future for their children. By joining the fight with radical Maoists during the long insurgency, people embraced new aspirations for change and dignity. When both sides of the political spectrum blatantly turned their backs on the people, the broader public rose in retaliation.

That was what triggered the September 2025 Gen Z protests. It was a powerful reminder to the rulers that people are the ultimate source of power and that they deserve a large share of the bounty. Ultimately, the electoral shift from one party to another between elections in the nation’s political market merely reflects the deeper cycle of hope and frustration in the economic sphere—a lesson today’s sitting politicians cannot afford to ignore.

articles.title: Why Nepal’s climate data is key to securing compensation
articles.summary:
The monsoon is back, bringing another series of disasters. According to the Department of Roads, five major highways are completely blocked across Nepal this week, with dozens of other road sections partially disrupted. The BP Highway connecting Kavrepalanchok and Sindhuli, a critical chokepoint linking eastern Nepal to the capital, is barely passable. Farmers in the Terai are anxious as the rain arrives late, leaving the soil harder for the next yield. One thing that remains common across these disasters is that there is no track record of data.

A few weeks ago, I was standing on the flooded bank of the Nakhu Khola in South Lalitpur with climate scientists from across the Hindu Kush Himalaya, including glaciologists, hydrologists and economists. We examined the visible evidence of climate change and observed a clear shift in the pattern, place and timing of rainfall that led to the 2024 floods. The historic Tika Bhairav temple, which stood since the Lichhavi era, was relocated.

There is no doubt that Nepal’s loss and damage is visible. The question is: How do we track and compile the evidence into a credible case? This matters because the available climate fund is not enough for mitigation and adaptation, and other countries that are bearing the brunt of climate change are queuing up with equally strong claims. The Global Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) was created to address economic and non-economic irreversible losses from climate change, for those affected the most. However, only $800 million has been pledged by the world’s largest emitters despite the dire need. More strikingly, 176 proposals have already arrived from 119 countries, with claims 11 times more than what is on the table. Every country is competing on the strength of the evidence it has gathered.

Nepal’s share of global emissions is a mere fraction of what its two neighbours, India and China, release in a single afternoon. Emissions do not respect boundaries, and glaciers are melting fast. Our rivers are flooding communities and farmers are losing harvests to a crisis largely manufactured elsewhere. The Loss and Damage fund exists precisely to bridge this asymmetry. Nepal has every right to compensation, but asserting it requires evidence.

Natural disasters have cost Nepal nearly $7 billion in cumulative damage in the past four decades. Every time, it is the community and families that bear the biggest burden of loss. The 2021 Melamchi flood caused an average loss of $52,000 per affected household, yet the government’s average relief payment was only $380. This is not an issue of funding alone but a clear sign of policy failure. Without systematic records, communities are provided with no evidence of climate losses that they rightfully owe.

The 2024 glacial flood in Thame burst devastated a Sherpa village in Khumbu that had stood for generations. In less than a year, a transboundary flash flood wiped away the Rasuwagadhi Friendship Bridge, which served as one of the important trade links with China. Nepal’s EV sector, growing as part of the country’s clean energy transition, took a direct hit too: our recent research using Nepal’s own customs data found the flood disrupted EV imports at a critical moment, exposing how climate risks can unravel mitigation efforts from the outside.

Despite millions in damage, the losses have not been compiled in any data system that could be referred to as a reference in future reconstruction efforts.

The non-economic losses, such as the loss of lives and livelihoods, displacement, destruction of cultural heritage, and long-term environmental impacts, are not even talked about. Nepal’s NDC 3.0 has quantified only physical infrastructure losses, at roughly $345 million. A country with Nepal’s disaster record should be at the front of the compensation queue. Instead, it keeps arriving at global climate summits without the paperwork to match its losses. What goes uncounted inevitably goes unclaimed.

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) runs a national hazard and damage-reporting portal called BIPAD. Its Forecast-Based Financing under the Anticipatory Action Framework releases cash to vulnerable households before floodwater arrives. But other than alerting you when to run, it tells you nothing about what was lost, what it was worth, nor whether the place you ran from should be rebuilt in the same spot.

So where does Nepal actually start? This June, Kathmandu Metropolitan City did something long overdue. It mapped 128 flood-prone locations and found over 8,000 households living at risk. This kind of granular local evidence is a good start for building the case for Loss and Damage financing. For the next step, these maps must be documented meticulously and converted into river embankments, relocated schools and ward-level evacuation plans before the next flood arrives. Only then can we build the evidence base for a future funding claim. Above all, the data must be shared across the sector so that climate risks are integrated in future development projects.

The Loss and Damage Fund is different from other climate funds that require multiple agencies, and aspires to reach communities directly. The data work, and the political will to do it, must start at the local level. The constitution has provided Nepal’s 753 local governments a strong legal mandate for disaster risk reduction. The challenge they face is the technical capacity to translate a hazard map into a tangible policy decision. The newly formed Green Climate Fund (GCF)-accredited national entities, such as the Town Development Fund, are already positioned to anchor local data tracking. What is still missing is a designated national authority with a clear mandate to manage and channel Loss and Damage funds when they arrive. A federal agency such as NDRRMA, which is already engaged in early warning and disaster response, could be ideal for the national coordination role.

It is not that Nepal has not engaged in climate policy. It was the first country to introduce climate budget tagging, but the issue lies in spending. Climate change recorded the lowest budget utilisation of any sector in FY2024-25. Systematic loss documentation needs its own dedicated budget line, not a token tag on someone else’s allocation. The case from Bhutan shows what happens when done patiently. A decade of quiet hydromet monitoring unlocked a $40 million disaster-resilience facility the country can draw on the moment a disaster strikes. The money always follows the data. Nepal is already a priority country in the global push to deliver Early Warnings for All by 2027, and warning is its clear strength. But warning and evidence are not the same achievement. What is required is the discipline to count what Nepal has already lost, and the institutional will to turn that count into a claim before the next funding window closes.

articles.title: Inside Arya Nishaant’s journey to becoming Miss Nepal International
articles.summary:
Arya Nishaant, Miss Nepal International 2026, was born and raised in Janakpur. She is a Business Administration graduate and Academic Coordinator by profession.

In this conversation with the Post’s Jony Nepal and Rivash Rijal, Nishaant discusses the friendships forged over high-stakes weeks of training, the exact second her name was called on crowning night, and why, in an industry built on being seen, she still believes the strongest thing a woman can have is a mind of her own.

What has been your biggest inspiration to start your pageantry journey?

My biggest inspirations to join pageantry were the international and national beauty queens I’ve seen growing up. I have seen the way pageantry has changed their lives, the impact they’ve brought to their society, the work they’ve done for other people, and the way they’ve helped others. I think all of that combined inspired me to join pageantry.

What was the most memorable and transformative part of your training sessions? How did you navigate self-improvement, growth, and self-criticism during the process?

I think the most memorable and fun part of our 50-day journey was making friends and spending time with them. We were together 24/7, on calls talking about what to do the next day, what’s happening, and how we could do better.

As for the transformative side, different aspects of us as humans were tested throughout the journey. Our intellect, the way we carry ourselves, how punctual we are, how we manage stress, because the days were long and stressful. We were also given constructive criticism to our faces, in front of everyone. That’s a hard pill to swallow. It’s different when suggestions come one-on-one versus in front of everyone. But I think that’s what helped everyone improve. It gave me a point to prove: that I can do better, and that's what helped me personally transform.

How do you curate a space in social media that drives real-world change while protecting your mental space from digital noise?

Before joining Miss Nepal, I had deleted all my socials. I am not someone who's very active on social media. If it were up to me, I would be living on a farm in a village with no internet. But as a pageant girl, there are certain things expected of you, and I had to have a social presence, so I did join.

I came in with a strong mindset. I am able to differentiate what's real life and what's ‘reel’ life. I don't let what anyone else has to say impact my mental health or how I see myself. I only take opinions from people who know me or know my journey. You just need a strong mindset to not let it get to you.

Take us back to the exact moment you were being crowned. What came to your mind, and who were you looking for in the crowd?

I didn't know my dad was going to attend the finale. I thought he would stay home with my mom, that it would just be my brother. I actually saw him in the crowd, and that really helped me stay grounded. I thought, ‘Okay, my dad is here; he’s watching me’. He was the one person I kept looking at throughout the time I was on stage.

At every step of the finale, I was so ready for my name not to be called. So when my name was called, it felt unreal. In the video, I don't think it looked like I had much emotion, but my heart was racing; I was breathing so heavily. I couldn't believe I was actually going to be one of those beauty queens with a crown on my head. It was magical.

A cause you’re passionate about?

Academics. I’ve been an academically inclined child my whole life, and education has played a very important role in shaping who my family and I have become. I think the lack of access to quality education in Nepal is one of the most prominent challenges I see, and my Beauty with a Purpose project is tied to that. It is something I want to keep working on.

What does the Miss Nepal community and sisterhood mean to you, and how has it shaped your journey?

I think the sisters we make throughout the Miss Nepal journey are the most important relationships to build, because it’s such a unique experience; if you don't have people who share the same experience to talk to, life can get very difficult. The friends we make during and after the journey keep us grounded and keep us sane.

How do you associate changemaking with pageantry? Could you have become a changemaker without it?

I don’t think pageantry and changemaking need to go hand in hand. You can be a changemaker regardless of whether or not you’re in pageantry. I think pageantry just accelerates the process. It helps you reach more people, connect with more people and organisations relevant to your cause. It’s a catalyst, not the reason change takes place.

What impact do you believe fashion can bring to self-expression and identity?

I believe fashion is a huge part of our personality and how we express ourselves. The way a person dresses shows how they see themselves and how others perceive them. Though for people who aren't into fashion and prefer comfort, that too reflects a personality that values practicality over being flashy.

For me, I love fashion. I have been designing and styling my own clothes, not professionally, but personally, and I really enjoy it. It's the message you give people without speaking, and especially in the industry we're in, it's important to carry yourself in a certain way and stay authentic to your personality.

What are your short-term and long-term goals?

Short-term, it's definitely to represent Nepal well. My international pageant is in four months, in November in Japan, and I need to prepare for that, give my best, and make my country proud.

Long-term, ideally I'd like to have a fashion business that also gives back to society, without needing to be actively hands-on with it. And for myself, to live on a sustainable farm.

A message for young people, particularly those aspiring to join pageantry?

You could take the route my friend Kashish (Miss Nepal Cosmo, 2026) took. She’s a professional model who's been in the industry a long time. Or you could do what I did. I modelled here and there, did about two shows in my whole life, and realised it was hampering my education, so I set it aside and focused on academics instead. I was a 4.0 student, and I took that route.

You could take the academic route or the professional route, whichever you're genuinely interested in. There isn’t a particular do's-and-don'ts list for becoming a beauty queen. If it's what you really want, first understand and research what's actually required of the pageant, and work on yourself accordingly.

articles.title: Miss Universe Nepal 2026 auditions conclude with 106 contestants
articles.summary:
The physical auditions for Miss Universe Nepal 2026, presented by Deepal, concluded at The Soaltee Kathmandu on Thursday. A total of 106 contestants from across Nepal and the Nepali diaspora vied for a place in the beauty pageant.

According to the organisers, the auditions attracted participants from various parts of the country as well as Non-Resident Nepalis living abroad. Contestants were evaluated on confidence, personality and talent as part of the selection process, organisers said.

A panel of judges will now shortlist the top 25 contestants, who will advance to the next stage of the competition. The finalists will participate in a series of grooming, mentorship and leadership development programmes designed to prepare them for the grand finale.

Organisers said the training will focus on enhancing the contestants’ communication skills, confidence and leadership qualities.

The winner of Miss Universe Nepal 2026 will earn the opportunity to represent Nepal at the international Miss Universe pageant.

articles.title: Miss Nepal World 2026 Deepmala Dhakal on turning a crown into cancer awareness platform
articles.summary:
From working as an investment strategist and holding a black belt in Taekwondo to delivering a TEDx talk and running marathons, Deepmala Dhakal, Miss Nepal World 2026, defies conventional stereotypes.

In a candid conversation with the Post’s Jony Nepal and Rivash Rijal, she reflects on her pageantry journey, navigating public scrutiny, and bringing global visibility to Nepal.

What was your biggest inspiration to begin your pageantry journey?

I knew I wanted to participate even before I was born because of my mother, who was a contestant in the very first Miss Nepal in 1994. Growing up outside Nepal, I did not relate to figures in the local Chinese limelight in Hong Kong; they didn’t look or sound like me. But in pageantry, I saw young women who walked with grace, carried immense presence, and spoke with absolute authority. That level of confidence inspired me, and I realised pageantry was where I could find my role models and discover who I wanted to become.

What was your training like, and how did you navigate the transition from self-improvement to self-criticism?

Stepping into a completely new format this year brought a lot of self-doubt. I questioned whether I still fit the mould, especially with the pressure of representing the Non-Resident Nepali (NRN) community on a global stage. The turning point occurred two weeks into the competition during the sash ceremony. I randomly drew contestant number 17—the exact number my mother held during her pageant in 1994 as a participant in the first Miss Nepal event. That moment felt like destiny. The fear instantly dissipated, giving me the mental resilience and confidence to stop doubting myself and focus entirely on growth.

Social media amplifies your voice, but it also subjects you to constant public evaluation. How do you drive real-world change while protecting your mental space?

It comes down to perspective. We seek the spotlight not for personal fame, but to accelerate our advocacy work. I accepted early on that public comment would follow every photo and challenge. As a second-generation NRN representing Hong Kong in Nepal, social media allowed me to connect with the diaspora.

I even posted videos speaking Nepali—something I had been self-conscious about due to my accent. Embracing my language publicly helped me overcome fear; ownership over identity leaves less room for criticism.

Have you ever felt the need to prove that beauty, intellect, and physical strength can coexist?

Yes. I strongly dislike the phrase ‘beauty with brains’ because it implicitly suggests that beauty usually exists without intelligence. They are not mutually exclusive. People often question why pageant contestants need lessons on walking, posture, or speaking. Historically in South Asian societies, women were expected to make themselves smaller and take up less space. Pageantry teaches women to walk with their chests out, hold their chins high, and claim their space. It is a comprehensive platform demonstrating that women can excel across all domains simultaneously.

Take us back to the moment you were crowned. What went through your mind, and what was your interaction with your mother?

The crowning moment was intense. Three titles were being awarded, and six of us held hands. As Miss International and Miss Cosmo were announced, I realised there was only one crown left for the remaining four of us—it became an all-or-nothing moment. Everything flashed through my head: the tireless dedication of my team, makeup artists, walk trainers, and community members in Hong Kong who volunteered their time to groom me.

When my name was called, it was pure relief. Because of stage protocol, my mother couldn’t come up immediately, but we held eye contact from across the stage. Right after winning, she was in complete disbelief, but in that shared look, we were fully connected and living in the moment.

What does the Miss Nepal sisterhood mean to you?

Coming from Hong Kong’s competitive environment, I initially approached the pageant with a purely performance-oriented mindset. The sisterhood was the sweetest surprise. As a naturally competitive person, I initially didn’t understand that sentiment. But being up there, I felt the exact same way. Shifted from trying to be the best to being my best, I viewed my peers’ strengths as inspiration rather than competition. If Nepal wins on the global stage, we all win.

How do pageantry and change-making intersect for you, and what is your primary advocacy?

Pageantry acts as a multiplier. Advocating for a cause individually might reach a hundred people, but wearing a crown brings a platform that reaches thousands. My primary advocacy is cancer awareness, inspired by losing my 30-year-old cousin brother to end-stage colon cancer after early symptoms were overlooked. Cancer affects one in five people; raising awareness about warning signs and early detection is genuinely life-saving work. As a goodwill ambassador for Nepal Cancer Hospital, this remains my core commitment, crown or no crown.

What are your short-term and long-term goals moving forward?

Short-term, my focus is entirely on preparing for Miss World. My fellow titleholders and I are putting in every effort to represent Nepal with dignity and achieve international recognition.

Long term, I am in Nepal to stay. I have relocated my life here and will continue my work with the NRNA. Professionally, I plan to maintain my career in finance, while also aspiring toward diplomacy. Given my international upbringing, multilingual background, and cross-cultural experience, diplomacy is a long-standing goal.

What is your message to young people and aspiring participants?

Take that initial step. Many young girls harbour dreams of pageantry or other high ambitions, but goals evolve as we grow. Whatever your goal is, do not get in your own way or yield to external noise. Understand your value, build steady momentum, and pursue your ambitions with your eyes wide open.

articles.title: मेक्सिकोमा ४३ विद्यार्थी बेपत्ता प्रकरणमा पूर्व गभर्नर पक्राउ
articles.summary:
मेक्सिकोमा सन् २०१४ मा ४३ जना विद्यार्थी बेपत्ता भएको चर्चित आयोत्जिनापा प्रकरणमा प्रमाण लुकाउने र अनुसन्धानलाई प्रभावित पार्ने आरोपमा तत्कालीन ग्युरेरो राज्यका पूर्वगभर्नर एन्जेल अगुइरे पक्राउ परेका छन्।

यो घटनालाई मेक्सिकोको भ्रष्टाचार, दण्डहीनता र जबर्जस्ती बेपत्ता पार्ने प्रवृत्तिको सबैभन्दा प्रतीकात्मक घटनामध्ये एक मानिन्छ।

सामान्य अभियोजक अर्नेस्टिना गोडोयका अनुसार अगुइरेले सरकारी कर्मचारी र उच्च तहका राज्य अधिकारीहरूको संलग्नतामा घटनासम्बन्धी प्रमाण लुकाउन निर्देशन दिएका थिए।

उनले उक्त कार्य कुनै व्यक्तिगत निर्णय नभई राज्य कार्यकारी तहबाट योजनाबद्ध रूपमा सञ्चालन गरिएको ढाकछोप अभियानको हिस्सा रहेको बताए।

आयोत्जिनापा ग्रामीण शिक्षक कलेजका ४३ जना विद्यार्थी सन् २०१४ सेप्टेम्बर २६ मा मेक्सिको सिटीमा हुने प्रदर्शनमा सहभागी हुन ग्युरेरो राज्यबाट यात्रा गरिरहेका बेला इगुआला सहरमा स्थानीय प्रहरीले उनीहरूलाई रोकेको थियो।

त्यसपछि भएको घण्टौँ लामो हिंसात्मक झडपमा छ जनाको मृत्यु भएको थियो भने ४३ जना विद्यार्थी बेपत्ता भएका थिए।

घटनापछि सरकारी अधिकारी, प्रहरी र अन्य व्यक्तिसहित दर्जनौँलाई पक्राउ गरिए पनि हालसम्म तीन जना विद्यार्थीको मात्र अवशेष फेला परेको छ। बाँकी ४० जनाको अवस्था अझै अज्ञात छ।

सत्तरी वर्षीय अगुइरेले उक्त घटनापछि सन् २०१४ मै बिदा लिएर आफ्नो कार्यकाल समाप्त हुनुअघि पद त्याग गरेका थिए।

पूर्वराष्ट्रपति एनरिक पेना निएटो नेतृत्वको सरकारले गरेको प्रारम्भिक अनुसन्धानले स्थानीय अधिकारी र लागुऔषध तस्करहरूको संलग्नतामा विद्यार्थीहरूको हत्या गरी शव जलाइएको निष्कर्ष निकालेको थियो।

तर त्यसपछिको सरकारले पुनः अनुसन्धान गर्दै घटनालाई ‘राज्य अपराध’ को संज्ञा दिएको थियो। सो अनुसन्धानले स्थानीय प्रहरी र आपराधिक समूहबीचको मिलेमतोमा विद्यार्थीहरूमाथि आक्रमण भएको निष्कर्ष प्रस्तुत गरेको थियो।

पीडित परिवारले लामो समयदेखि मेक्सिकोको सेनासमेत घटनामा संलग्न रहेको आरोप लगाउँदै आएका छन्।

सन् २०२२ मा एक जना जनरलसहित तीन सैनिकलाई पक्राउ गरिएको थियो भने सन् २०२३ मा स्वतन्त्र अनुसन्धान आयोगले सेनाले महत्त्वपूर्ण प्रमाण लुकाएको आरोप लगाएको थियो।

हाल यो बहुचर्चित आयोत्जिनापा मुद्दा राष्ट्रपति क्लाउडिया सेनबाम नेतृत्वको सरकारको जिम्मेवारीमा रहेको छ।

उनले सत्य पत्ता लगाउने, न्याय सुनिश्चित गर्ने र बेपत्ता विद्यार्थीहरूको अवस्थाबारे वास्तविकता सार्वजनिक गर्ने प्रतिबद्धता व्यक्त गरेका छन्।

articles.title: सुनको मूल्य फेरि उकालो
articles.summary:
नेपाली बजारमा शुक्रबार सुनको मूल्य सामान्य वृद्धि भएको छ। नेपाल सुनचाँदी व्यवसायी महासंघका अनुसार आज सुन प्रतितोला २ लाख ९६ हजार ९ सय रुपैयाँमा कारोबार भइरहेको छ।

बिहीबार सुनको मूल्य प्रतितोला २ लाख ९६ हजार रुपैयाँ कायम भएको थियो। बिहिबारको तुलनामा आज सुनको मूल्य प्रतितोला ९ सय रुपैयाँले बढेको हो।

यसैबीच, चाँदीको मूल्यमा चाँदी प्रतितोला १० रुपैयाँले बढेर ४ हजार ५८० रुपैयाँमा कारोबार भइरहेको महासंघले जनाएको छ। बिहिबार चाँदीको मूल्य प्रतितोला ४ हजार ५७० रुपैयाँ रहेको थियो।

articles.title: टिक्दैन नियन्त्रित लोकतन्त्र
articles.summary:
सुनसरी–सिरहाका घटना अत्यन्तै दुःखद हुन्। सुरक्षाकर्मीका असावधानीका नतिजा थिए ती। मृत्युसंख्या र परिस्थिति फरक थिए तर चैत्र १५ को तीनकुने र भदौ २३–२४ का हत्या, आगजनी र लुटपाटका प्रकृति उस्तै हुन्। सरकार, व्यापारी प्रतिष्ठान र निजी सम्पत्ति तारो बने। कम्मरमाथि गोली चले। राहत र दोषीलाई उन्मुक्ति दिएर दिगो शान्ति हुँदैन। ‘संक्रमणकालीन न्याय’लाई सम्बोधन नगरेबाट देश ‘दण्डहीनताको स्वर्गभूमि’ बनेको नकार्न पनि मिल्दैन।

असन्तुष्टि चुलिएपछि पटक–पटक मुलुकमा क्रान्ति र आन्दोलन भए। राज्यको अकर्मण्यताले नागरिकले ज्यान गुमाए। सहिद र क्षतिपूर्ति घोषणा, उपचार र रोजगारीका आश्वासन बाँडिए। छानबिन आयोग बन्ने, प्रतिवेदन बुझाउने तर सार्वजनिक नहुने रोग लागिरह्यो। भइहाले पनि सिफारिस लागु हुँदैनन्। यो कुचक्र तीन दशकदेखि चलेको छ। सम्भवतः कप्तानगन्ज घटनाले पनि यही नियति भोग्ला। दोषी व्यक्ति प्रधानमन्त्री, मन्त्री, सुरक्षा निकायका प्रमुख र उच्च सरकारी ओहदामा पुगे। पीडितलाई गिज्याइरहे।

साउन १० गते सुनसरीको कप्तानगन्जबाट सल्किएको हिंसा विभिन्न जिल्लामा फैलियो। प्रत्यक्षदर्शीअनुसार मुस्लिम र हिन्दुबिच केही विवाद भयो तर मुठभेड भएको थिएन। यस क्षेत्रमा हिन्दु र मुसलमानबिच कहिल्यै दंगा भएको थिएन।

प्रहरी र बोलबम पक्षबिच झडप भयो। सुरक्षाकर्मीको असावधानीबाट अवस्था भयावह बन्यो। चार निर्दोष नागरिकले ज्यान गुमाए। एक दर्जनभन्दा बढी घाइते भए तर यस घटनालाई हिन्दु–मुस्लिमबिचको दंगा भनी दुष्प्रचार गरियो। सेनासमेत परिचालित भए।

गृहमन्त्रालयले छानबिन समिति बनायो। हुलदंगा नरोकिएपछि ‘मौन प्रधानमन्त्री’ले राष्ट्रका नाममा सम्बोधन गरे। राष्ट्रपतिलाई भेटेर घटनाको जानकारी दिए। चार दिनदेखि बेखबर गृहमन्त्रीलाई संवादबाट निकास खोज्न तराई झारे। दल, नागरिक समाज, धार्मिक गुरु तथा अन्य संघ–संस्थासित सहयोगको अपिल गरे। दमनको बाटो छाडी संवाद र सद्भावको मार्ग रोजे। सरकार एक्लिएर समाधान ननिस्कने देखे। बल प्रयोगबाट राजनीति नचल्ने बुझे।

२०६४ भदौ ३० गते कपिलवस्तुको चन्द्रौटामा मुस्लिमका अगुवा अब्दुल मोइद खाँको अज्ञात समूहबाट हत्या भएको थियो। साम्प्रदायिक हिंसा भड्कियो र १४ जनाले ज्यान गुमाए। आगजनी, लुटपाट र बलात्कारजस्ता जघन्य अपराध भए। न्यायाधीश लोकेन्द्र मल्लिकको संयोजनमा न्यायिक छानबिन समिति बन्यो, प्रतिवेदन पनि बुझायो तर त्यो न सार्वजनिक भयो, न त लागु।

यसको करिब नौ महिनाअघि (२०६३ पुस ८–१२) नेपालगन्जमा सद्भावना पार्टीको ‘बन्द’ साम्प्रदायिक दंगामा बदलियो। मधेसी–पहाडे झडपमा परिणत भयो। त्यसबेला पनि प्रहरी प्रशासनका लापरबाहीबाट एक युवाको हत्या भएपछि सहर हिंसाको चपेटामा पर्‍यो। आगजनी, लुटपाटसहित कैयौं व्यक्ति घाइते भए। पछि नागरिक समाजको सहजीकरणबाट दुवै घटना तत्कालका लागि शान्त भयो। तथापि कुनै पनि दोषीले आजसम्म सजाय पाएका छैनन्।

यतिबेला रास्वपाका वरिष्ठ नेता तथा मधेसीमूलका बालेन्द्र शाह मुलुकका प्रधानमन्त्री छन्। सत्ता सम्हालेको चार महिना पुग्दा नपुग्दै मधेसमा हिंसा भड्कियो। आगजनी तथा लुटपाटले आक्रान्त भयो। मुस्लिम समुदाय सन्त्रासमा छन्। सदियौंदेखि मिलिजुली बसेका समुदायबिच घृणा फैलाइएको छ। भ्रामक सूचनाले मानसिक तनाव बढाएको छ। ‘सम्मानपूर्वक बाँच्न पाउने’ मौलिक हक कुण्ठित छ। तथापि एकता, सहिष्णुता, सद्भावबाट मात्र समाज अघि बढ्ने नागरिक समाजका प्रयासले काम गर्‍यो। प्रधानमन्त्रीको सम्बोधन र गृहमन्त्रीका पीडितसँगको भेटघाटले वातावरण सहज बन्दै छ।

विडम्बना, प्रधानमन्त्री बालेन्द्र शाह लोकतन्त्रका पहरेदार देखिएनन्। संसद्प्रति जवाफदेही भएका छैनन्। तराईमा भएका जनधनको क्षति, आगजनी, लुटपाट तथा विध्वंसका घटनाबारे संसद्लाई जानकारी दिएका छैनन्। अध्यक्ष रवि लामिछानेले बोलाएको सर्वदलीय बैठकमा न आफू गए, न त गृहमन्त्रीलाई पठाए। नेपाली कांग्रेसका सभापति गगन थापाले प्रश्न गरे, ‘यस्तो बेलामा पनि प्रधानमन्त्रीले भाउ खाने हो ?’

प्रधानमन्त्री शाह ‘नियन्त्रित लोकतन्त्र’का शैलीबाट अघि बढेका छन्। न्यायालय र संवैधानिक अंगलाई नियन्त्रणमा राख्ने चेष्टामा छन्। निजी मिडियालाई आर्थिक नाकाबन्दीमा पारेका छन्। अध्यादेशबाट संवैधानिक परिषद् ऐन संशोधन गरी सिफारिसका चौथो व्यक्तिलाई प्रधानन्यायाधीश बनाए। निर्वाचन आयोगमा अनुकूल व्यक्ति पठाए। देखावटी प्रतिस्पर्धामा सरकारी नियुक्ति गरे। संसद् र संसदीय समितिलाई सरकारी छाया बनाए। ओली सरकारलाई मात दिने गरी शासन चलाए तर रास्वपा भने ‘मौन’ छ।

विष्णु पौडेल विशेष अदालतको आदेशमा छुटेपछि ‘बालेन’ले न्यायाधीशलाई थर्काउने अशोभनीय ‘स्टेटस’ लेखे। यसअघि पनि सरकारविरुद्धका फैसलामा न्यायाधीशमाथि आक्रोश पोखेर यस क्षेत्रमा त्रास फैलाएका छन्। केही हप्ताअघि एम्नेस्टी इन्टरनेसनल, ह्युमन राइट्स वाच र आइसिजे अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय अधिकारवादी संस्थाले अदालतको स्वतन्त्रता र निष्पक्षतामाथि आँच पुर्‍याउने कार्यप्रति विश्वको ध्यानाकर्षण गराए। प्रधानन्यायाधीशको नियुक्तिमा रोलक्रम मिचिएको, तीन न्यायाधीशमाथि राजीनामा र महाभियोगका दबाब विश्वसनीय रिपोर्टबाट प्राप्त भएको एक विज्ञप्ति सार्वजनिक गरेका थिए।

यी संस्था कुनै पनि देशको संसद्प्रति जवाफदेही हुँदैनन् तर न्याय, कानुन तथा मानव अधिकार संसदीय समिति सक्रिय भयो। यस विषयमा सरकारसँग सत्यतथ्य र जवाफ माग्नुपर्नेमा उल्टै सूचना सार्वजनिक गर्ने संस्थाहरूमाथि कारबाहीको मनसायले सम्बन्धित निकायलाई हास्यास्पद र गैरजिम्मेवार निर्देशन दिने निर्णय गर्‍यो। हेक्का रहोस्, न्याय तथा मानव अधिकार घरेलु मामला मात्र हुँदैनन्, अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय चासो र चिन्ताका विषय पनि हुन्।

अख्तियार दुरुपयोग अनुसन्धान आयोगका पदाधिकारीलाई सिंहदरबारमा बोलाएर थुन्न र मुद्दा चलाउन दिएका दबाब खुलिसकेको छ। पाँच घण्टा त के, पाँच वर्ष अख्तियारलाई नछोड्ने चितवन महाधिवेशनबाट उद्घोष गरेबाट यसको पुष्टि हुन्छ। यसबाट अन्य संवैधानिक आयोग पनि दबाबमा छन्। लोकतन्त्रका आधारभूत मर्म शक्तिपृथकीकरण ध्वस्त पारिँदै छ। ‘एक्सप्रेस वे’मा अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय प्रतिबद्धता, संविधान र कानुन मिचेर अघि बढ्ने संकेत गरेका छन् तर यो सम्भव छैन। सिंगो नागरिक समाजसमेत यसका विरुद्धमा खरो गरी उत्रनेछ।

भ्रष्टाचारीलाई कारबाही गर्न शाह जति दृढ छन्, अपराधीका सजायमा उति नै उदासीन। गौरीबहादुर कार्की प्रतिवेदन र राष्ट्रिय मानव अधिकार आयोगका सिफारिस बेवास्ता यसको प्रमाण हो। थाती रहेको संक्रमणकालीन न्याय प्रक्रियामा द्वन्द्वपीडितलाई ‘बाइपास’ गरेर अघि बढ्ने ढाँचा ‘जुन जोगी आए पनि कानै चिरेको’ हुनु हो। यसर्थ दिगो शान्ति र दण्डहीनता अन्त्यका पूर्वसर्त, पीडित केन्द्रित प्रक्रियालाई अघि बढाउनु हो।

सद्भाव तथा भाइचाराका प्रेरणाका स्रोत प्रधानमन्त्री र मन्त्री पनि हुन् तर तिनका ‘स्टेटस’ तथा अभिव्यक्तिबाट त्यस्तो देखिन्न। विशेषगरी ‘देश बनाउने टिम’का अभिव्यक्ति आपत्तिजनक छन्। लामो समयदेखि ‘बालेन्द्र’को एकाउन्टबाट आउने स्टेटस प्रायः विगतका नेतृत्व, विपक्षी सांसद, न्यायाधीश तथा कर्मचारीप्रति घृणाका भाव हुन्छन्। यसबाट सर्वसाधारणमा कस्तो प्रभाव पर्ला ? नागरिकबिच विभाजन र द्वेष फैलाउने कारक बन्छ÷बन्दैन ? ३५ वर्षे शासनकालमा भएका असल कार्यको प्रशंसा गर्दा आपसी सम्मान र सौहार्द नै बढाउँछ।

‘बालेन’ यतिबेला प्रधानमन्त्री बालेन्द्र शाह भएका छन्। उनका अनुशासित व्यवहारले राष्ट्रको मान र प्रतिष्ठा बढ्ने हो। ‘एक्लो बालेन भर्सेस अल’ सोच इतिहास भएको छ।

articles.title: भन्सार छलेर ल्याइएका सामानसहित चार जना पक्राउ
articles.summary:
कञ्चनपुर प्रहरीले भारतबाट भन्सार छलेर नेपाल भित्र्याउन लागेका सामानसहित चार जना भारतीयलाई पक्राउ गरेको छ।

बेलौरी नगरपालिका–१ खल्लाबाट भन्सार छलेर नेपाल भित्र्याउन लागेको रु ५७ हजार बराबरको तीन क्विन्टल ५० किलो तोरी र चार थान साइकलसहित उनीहरूलाई बिहीबार नियन्त्रणमा लिइएको हो। जिल्ला प्रहरी कार्यालयका प्रवक्ता टेकबहादुर रावतका अनुुसार भारतबाट भन्सार छली ल्याइएका रु २५ हजार बराबरका पेय पदार्थ, बिडी, बोइलर कुखुरा बेलौरी नगरपालिका– २ बैजुडाँडा फालिएको अवस्थामा भेटिएका छन्।

सामान पनि स्थानीय टेडुवा प्रहरीचौकीले बेवारिसे अवस्थामा फेला पारेको जनाएको छ। यसैबीच, जुवाको खालबाट आठ जना पक्राउ परेका छन्। उनीहरूबाट नगद रु ५५ हजार पनि बरामद भएको छ ।

articles.title: सरकारले जनताको भावना बुझ्न सकेन : आङदेम्बे
articles.summary:
नेपाली कांग्रेसका संसदीय दलका नेता भीष्मराज आङदेम्बेले सरकारले जनताको आवाज उठाउन नसकेको आरोप लगाएका छन्।

शुक्रबार पार्टी निकट आदिवासी जनजाति महासंघको कार्यक्रममा बोल्दै नेता आङदेम्बेले सरकारले आदिवासी जनजाति, दलित, महिला र गरिब किसानको संवेदनशीलता बुझ्न नसकेको बताए।

उनले भने,‘सिंहदरबार भित्र देखिएको बहुमतले आदिवासी जनजाति, दलित, महिला र गरिब किसानको संवेदनशीलता बुझ्न सकेको छैन। यो सरकार नैतिक धरातलमा उभिएको छैन।’

यस्तै, उनले जस्तोसुकै प्रतिकूल परिस्थिति आएपनि नेपाली कांग्रेसको लक्ष्य र उद्देश्यमा विचलित नहुने बताए।

उनले कांग्रेसले मुलुकको सबै भूगोल र समुदायको संवेदनशीलतालाई सम्बोधन गर्ने बताए।

articles.title: प्रधानमन्त्रीको अभिव्यक्ति रेकर्डबाट हटाउन माग
articles.summary:
नेपाल कम्युनिष्ट पार्टी (नेकपा) का सांसद युवराज दुलालले प्रधानमन्त्रीको विवादास्पद अभिव्यक्ति संसदको रेकर्डबाट हटाउन माग गर्दै तातोपानी नाका र अरनिको राजमार्ग तत्काल सञ्चालनमा ल्याउन सरकारसँग आग्रह गरेका छन्।

शुक्रबार प्रतिनिधिसभाको बैठकमा बोल्दै सांसद दुलालले प्रधानमन्त्रीले संसदमा दिएको ‘नेपालले पनि भारतको धेरै ठाउँमा जग्गा मिचेको छ’ भन्ने अभिव्यक्तिलाई सच्याउन, स्पष्ट पार्न वा संसदको अभिलेखबाट हटाउन आफूहरू लामो समयदेखि माग गर्दै आएको बताए।

उनले राष्ट्रियताको विषयमा कुनै सम्झौता हुन नसक्ने उल्लेख गर्दै उक्त अभिव्यक्ति संसदको रेकर्डमा राख्न नहुने धारणा राखे। प्रधानमन्त्रीलाई संसदमा उपस्थित गराई जवाफ दिन लगाउन वा सभामुखले यस विषयमा रुलिङ गर्नुपर्ने उनको माग थियो।

‘यो सदनमा हामीले लामो समयदेखि सम्माननीय प्रधानमन्त्रीज्यूले संसदमा आएर बोल्दा ‘नेपालले पनि भारतको धेरै ठाउँमा जग्गा मिचेको छ’ भन्ने अभिव्यक्तिलाई सच्याउन, स्पष्टीकरण दिन अथवा रेकर्डबाट हटाउन माग गर्दै आएका छौं। यो राष्ट्रियताको सवाल हो, हाम्रो जमिनको सवाल हो। हामी राष्ट्रका लागि आवश्यक पर्दा रगत बगाउन सक्छौं, शिर बलिदान गर्न सक्छौं, तर राज्यप्रतिको विवादास्पद भनाइलाई राष्ट्रिय रेकर्डमा राख्न सक्दैनौं। त्यसैले सभामुखमार्फत प्रधानमन्त्रीलाई संसदमा बोलाइयोस् वा रुलिङ गरेर उक्त अभिव्यक्ति रेकर्डबाट हटाइयोस्,’ उनले भने ।

सांसद दुलालले एक महिनादेखि पहिरोका कारण अवरुद्ध रहेको तातोपानी नाका र अरनिको राजमार्ग तत्काल सञ्चालनमा ल्याउन पनि सरकारको ध्यानाकर्षण गराए। डाक्लाङ, इको र लिपिङ क्षेत्रमा गएको पहिरोका कारण सडक बन्द हुँदा भोटेकोशी गाउँपालिकाको जनजीवन कष्टकर बनेको र चीनसँगको प्रमुख व्यापारिक मार्ग अवरुद्ध हुँदा व्यापारीहरूले ठूलो आर्थिक क्षति बेहोर्नुपरेको उनले बताए।

उनले केही साताअघि मन्त्रीहरू, राष्ट्रिय योजना आयोगका उपाध्यक्ष तथा उच्च सरकारी अधिकारीहरूको टोलीले स्थलगत निरीक्षण गरे पनि सडक सञ्चालनका लागि प्रभावकारी पहल नभएको भन्दै सरकारको कार्यशैलीमाथि प्रश्न उठाए। उनले सरकारले विपद् व्यवस्थापनभन्दा ‘विपद् पर्यटन’ मा बढी ध्यान दिएको जस्तो देखिएको टिप्पणी गरे।

‘एक महिनादेखि तातोपानी नाका बन्द हुँदा भोटेकोशी गाउँपालिका नै सडक यातायातबाट विच्छेद भएको छ। मन्त्रीहरू र उच्च अधिकारीहरूको टोली निरीक्षणमा पुग्यो, तर आजसम्म सडक सञ्चालन गर्ने तदारुकता देखिएको छैन। सरकार विपद् व्यवस्थापन गर्न गएको हो कि विपद् पर्यटन गर्न गएको हो भन्ने प्रश्न उठेको छ। त्यसैले अबिलम्ब तातोपानी नाका र अरनिको लोकमार्ग खुला गरियोस्, सडक मर्मत गरियोस् र जनजीवन सहज बनाइयोस्,’ उनले भने ।

त्यस्तै, सिन्धुपाल्चोकको जुगल गाउँपालिकास्थित निर्माणाधीन अपर बलेफी ‘ए’ जलविद्युत् आयोजनामा असार १४ गतेदेखि बेपत्ता भएका हेलम्बु–५ का अमरे तामाङको खोजी कार्य केन्द्रबाट प्रहरी परिचालन गरी तीव्र बनाउन सरकारसँग आग्रह गरे।

articles.title: संसदको गतिरोध छिट्टै अन्त्य गर्न सांसद राईको आग्रह
articles.summary:
श्रमसंस्कृति पार्टीका सांसद ध्रुवराज राईले लामो समयदेखि जारी संसद्को गतिरोध अन्त्य गरी जनताका मुद्दामा केन्द्रित हुन सबै राजनीतिक दललाई आग्रह गरेका छन्। उनले निरन्तरको अवरोधले संसद्को समय खेर गएको र जनतामा गलत सन्देश गएको बताए।

शुक्रबार बसेको प्रतिनिधिसभा बैठकमा बोल्दै सांसद राईले संसद् अवरुद्ध भइरहँदा जनताले आफ्ना प्रतिनिधिलाई हेरिरहेको भन्दै जतिसक्दो छिटो राजनीतिक सहमतिमार्फत निकास निकाल्नुपर्ने बताए।

उनले भने, ‘म चाहिँ यो विषयमा अगाडिदेखि नै सकेभर छिटो टुङ्ग्याऔँ भन्ने पक्षमा छु। जनताले तपाईं–हामीलाई उनीहरूको प्रतिनिधि बनाएर पठाएका हुन्। उहाँहरू हामीलाई हेरिरहनुभएको छ। यस्तो अवस्थामा हामीले कति वर्षसम्म यही विषयमा मात्रै छलफल गरिरहने ? समस्याको समाधान खोज्नैपर्छ।’

उनले संसदमा आफ्नो पार्टीले संकल्प प्रस्तावसमेत अघि सारेको स्मरण गर्दै राजनीतिक दलहरूले एकअर्कालाई दोषारोपण गर्नेभन्दा समाधानमा केन्द्रित हुनुपर्ने धारणा राखे।

उनले भने, ‘देशलाई माया गर्ने हो भने कसले के भन्यो भनेर मात्र बस्ने होइन, समाधान खोज्नुपर्छ। मान्छेबाट गल्ती हुन सक्छ, तर गल्ती स्वीकार गरेर समस्याको निकास निकाल्नुपर्छ। समाधान नखोज्ने हो भने हामी कहिलेसम्म यही ढंगले अघि बढ्ने ?’

दलका नेता, प्रधानमन्त्री र सभामुखबीच छलफलमार्फत छिट्टै निष्कर्ष निकाल्नुपर्ने आवश्यकता औंल्याउँदै उनले संसद् सञ्चालनलाई प्रभावकारी बनाउन आग्रह गरे।

उनले भने, ‘दुई–दुई महिना सदन अवरुद्ध भइरहने हो भने बरु दलका नेता, प्रधानमन्त्री र सभामुख बसेर यसको निष्कर्ष निकाल्नुपर्छ। यसको समाधान सडकमा होइन, यही संसद्भित्र खोजिनुपर्छ।’

सांसद राईले संसद् अवरोधका कारण समय र स्रोतको दुरुपयोग भइरहेको उल्लेख गर्दै सांसदहरूले आफ्नो समय जनताका समस्या उठाउन खर्चिनुपर्ने बताए।

उनले भने, ‘एक जना सांसदले चार मिनेट मात्रै बोल्दा पनि हरेक बैठकमा हामीले कति समय खेर फालिरहेका छौँ भन्ने हिसाब गर्नुपर्छ। यो जनताको अपेक्षाअनुसारको काम होइन।’

सरकारले दिएको स्पष्टीकरणबारे आफूहरूले अध्ययन गरेको उल्लेख गर्दै उनले उठाइएका विषयको अझै प्रभावकारी समाधान हुन नसकेको बताए।

उनले भने, ‘सरकारले दिएको स्पष्टीकरणका विषयमा हामीले अध्ययन गरेका छौँ। जनताले पनि सबै कुरा देखिरहनुभएको छ। धेरै विषय उठे, तर अहिलेसम्म त्यसको उचित समाधान भएको छैन भन्ने हाम्रो निष्कर्ष छ। त्यसैले सभामुखज्यूको पहलमा समस्याको समाधानको एउटा बिन्दु खोजौँ। संसद्लाई फेरि दुर्गन्धित बनाउने होइन, निकास दिने बाटो खोज्नुपर्छ।’

articles.title: सरकारमा बहुमतको अहंकार देखियो : गगन थापा
articles.summary:
नेपाली कांग्रेसका सभापति गगनकुमार थापाले सरकार अराजक शैलीमा अगाडी बढिरहेको आरोप लगाएका छन्।

शुक्रबार पार्टी निकट आदिवासी जनजाति महासंघको कार्यक्रममा बोल्दै सभापति थापाले सरकारको कार्यशैली र मन्त्रीहरुको अभिव्यक्तिप्रति असन्तुष्टि जनाए।

कानुनभन्दा माथि कोही पनि हुन नसक्ने बताउँदै उनले मन्त्री र सांसदहरूको उत्तेजक तथा धम्कीपूर्ण अभिव्यक्ति विधिको शासनमाथि चुनौती भएको बताए।

‘वर्तमान सरकारमा प्रचण्ड बहुमतको अहंकार देखिएको छ। जसका कारण शासकीय अराजकता निम्तिएको छ’ उनले भने,‘ मुख्य व्यक्तिको कार्यशैली नै अराजक भएपछि त्यसको प्रभाव तल्लो तहसम्म पुगेको छ। अहिले नागरिकहरूमा ठूलो आक्रोश छ।’

यस्तै, उनले विभिन्न माग राखेर आन्दोलनरत पक्षसँग सरकारले गरेका सम्झौता कार्यान्वयन नभएको भन्दै आपत्ती जनाए। उनले जनताका समस्या समाधानमा सरकार गम्भीर नदेखिएको आरोप लगाए।

articles.title: How Nepal’s tax lottery works—and how a Rs250 purchase won Rs1 million
articles.summary:
A consumer who spent just Rs250 at a grocery store in Kanchanpur has won the government’s Rs1 million bumper prize under its new taxpayer incentive lottery programme, with the first winners announced on Friday. The winner bought the goods from Shiva Krishna General Store in Punarbas Municipality, according to the Inland Revenue Department.

How does the lottery work?

The prize is part of a government programme designed to encourage consumers to ask for bills and promote transparent transactions. According to the procedure, anyone making a personal purchase of goods or services worth more than Rs100 in a single transaction is eligible to participate. This excludes commercial purchases, transport, airfares and transactions with non-PAN/VAT vendors.

On Friday, 15 consumers won daily prizes of Rs100,000 each (Rs133,334 before tax), while one consumer was selected for the Rs1 million bumper prize (Rs750,000 after tax). The prize money will be subject to applicable taxes. The winners were selected from among 25.60 million electronic transactions and 7,077 cash transactions.

The winners were selected using the “cryptographically secure uniform random sampling without replacement” method. This ensures that every coupon has an equal chance of being selected, that the same coupon cannot be selected more than once in a single draw, and that the selection process remains completely fair and secure.

According to the Inland Revenue Department, there are over 7 million taxpayers in Nepal, most of them individuals holding personal Permanent Account Numbers (PAN). Similarly, there are around 193,724 business PAN holders, 338,316 businesses registered for Value Added Tax (VAT), and 121,682 excise duty licence holders.

Why has the government introduced the lottery?

The programme is intended to encourage consumers to demand official bills whenever they purchase goods and services. By increasing consumer demand for bills, the government hopes to discourage businesses from hiding sales and underreporting their income, thereby improving tax compliance.

Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle announced the taxpayer incentive programme in the federal budget for fiscal year 2026-27. The idea is to turn consumers into an additional layer of tax monitoring by giving them a financial incentive to insist on documented transactions.

Winners will be selected through a computerised system in the presence of senior government officials, invited dignitaries and media representatives.

Keshav Raghuvanshi, information officer at the Inland Revenue Department, said the programme is designed to encourage consumers to ask for tax invoices, improve the recording of business transactions and strengthen tax compliance.

Who can participate in the lottery?

Consumers who purchase goods or services and make payments through digital channels such as QR are automatically entered into the programme. However, they must keep their purchase bills if they win a prize.

Consumers paying in cash can also participate, but they have to take a PAN or VAT bill from the seller and upload it through the Inland Revenue Department’s website. After uploading the bill, they receive a prize coupon that makes them eligible for the lottery. The programme covers purchases made between July 17 and July 31 for the first draw.

How are the winners selected?

The government will conduct the prize draw twice a month. The prizes will be announced on the 16th day of each Nepali month for purchases made from the first to the 15th day, and on the final day of the month for purchases made during the remaining days.

The 15 daily winners are selected separately from transactions made on each of the 15 days. The bumper prize, however, is drawn from all eligible consumers who made purchases during the first half of the Nepali month. The Inland Revenue Department is responsible for the technical arrangements for the lottery system.

What does the programme mean for consumers and businesses?

For consumers, the programme provides a chance to win cash simply by asking for proof of purchase and using formal payment channels. More importantly, the government expects the incentive to make consumers more conscious of obtaining bills.

For businesses, greater demand for PAN and VAT bills could make it harder to conceal sales and evade taxes. The government hopes that this consumer-driven pressure will encourage more transparent transactions and improve tax compliance.

How are winners notified?

The department will notify winners by SMS and email and publish their names on its official website and social media platforms.

Prize winners must submit their claims within 15 days of the announcement at the nearest Inland Revenue Office. They will be required to produce the original tax invoice, a citizenship certificate, national identity card, passport or driving licence, bank account details and a PAN card.

A 25 percent windfall tax will be deducted from the prize before payment, in accordance with Nepal’s tax laws. The remaining amount will be deposited into the winner’s bank account within 10 days after verification of the required documents.

Any unclaimed prize money will be transferred to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund.

articles.title: Eight of Kalikot’s nine local units face high landslide risk
articles.summary:
A district disaster preparedness assessment has identified eight of Kalikot’s nine local units as being at high risk of landslides, with only Raskot Municipality classified as facing a moderate risk.

Authorities say the threat is being driven not only by the district’s fragile geology but also by the rapid expansion of poorly engineered rural roads, which have destabilised hillsides and increased the likelihood of slope failures.

Chief District Officer Jhabilal Bhattarai said landslides occur across the district because of its weak geological formation, but unplanned road construction by local units has significantly worsened the risk.

The Karnali Highway and the Karnali Corridor, two of the region’s key transport routes, are repeatedly blocked by landslides whenever heavy rain falls, disrupting travel and the movement of essential supplies.

To improve disaster preparedness, the district has prepared the District Disaster Preparedness and Response Plan 2026, covering a wide range of hazards including floods, landslides, fires, epidemics, drought, lightning, windstorms, falls from cliffs and rockfalls.

The plan, prepared under the leadership of the District Disaster Management Committee, has secured commitments from government agencies, local units and development organisations for its implementation, Bhattarai said.

Assistant chief district officer Janak Sharma said the district has identified landslides, floods, fires, drought, windstorms, hailstorms, epidemics, lightning, falls from cliffs, rockfalls, road accidents and attacks by wild animals as its major disaster risks.

He said authorities have mapped settlements facing the greatest landslide threat and are working through local governments to raise public awareness and strengthen community preparedness.

Kalikot is also highly vulnerable to earthquakes because of its fragile terrain, said Bal Prasad Sanjyal, a member of the District Disaster Management Committee and president of the Kalikot chapter of the Nepal Red Cross Society.

He said strict enforcement of Nepal’s National Building Code is essential for all new construction, arguing that compliance with building standards could significantly reduce casualties and property damage during future disasters.

The district administration, working with the Nepal Police, the Nepali Army and the Armed Police Force, has also expanded search-and-rescue training, emergency information management and disaster response capacity.

The preparedness plan includes stockpiling rescue equipment and strengthening one-door emergency operation centres operated by local units.

Authorities have identified 33 safe evacuation sites across all nine local units to facilitate rescue operations during disasters. Potential helicopter landing sites have also been designated to support emergency evacuations and relief operations if roads become impassable.

The district disaster preparedness and response plan has been distributed to the Ministry of Home Affairs, all local units and other relevant agencies.

Deputy Superintendent of Police Him Bahadur Khatri, chief of the District Police Office, said the plan is intended to ensure that available resources can be mobilised quickly and effectively during emergencies.

The District Disaster Management Committee has identified several settlements as among the district’s most landslide-prone areas. These include Rupsa and Malkot in Naraharinath Rural Municipality; Poriban, Palata and Khardu in Sanni Tribeni Rural Municipality; Garuwa and Siyala in Khandachakra Municipality; and Dahachaur and Samalagaun in Shubha Kalika Rural Municipality.

Settlements along the Tila and Karnali rivers, as well as those near the Rahagad, Sannigad, Phugad, Tibgad, Damrigad, Simlagad, Baligad, Padamgad, Takulla, Bali and Khallagad streams, have also been listed as areas vulnerable to flooding and landslides.

articles.title: पत्रकार धनबल राई 'धनकेशर-अतम्हरी राई स्मृति पत्रकारिता पुरस्कार'बाट सम्मानित
articles.summary:
'धनकेशर-अतम्हरी राई स्मृति पत्रकारिता पुरस्कार' पत्रकार धनबल राईलाई प्रदान गरिएको छ।

पत्रकार राई किरात राई यायोक्खाको ३९औं स्थापना दिवसका अवसरमा 'धनकेशर-अतम्हरी राई स्मृति पत्रकारिता पुरस्कार'बाट नगद २५ हजारसहित ताम्रपत्रका साथ पत्रकार राईलाई सम्मान गरिएको हो।

शुक्रबार यायोक्खाको स्थापना दिवसका अवसरमा ललितपुरमा आयोजित एक समारोहका बीच यायोक्खा केन्द्रीय अध्यक्ष जीवन हाताचोबाट पत्रकार राई सम्मानित भएका हुन्।

एक दशकभन्दा अगाडिदेखि पत्रकारिता गरिरहेका राईले नागरिक दैनिकसहित विभिन्न अनलाईन, टेलिभिजन र रेडियोमा काम गरेका छन्।

articles.title: अस्पतालभित्र इन्टरनेट चलाउन आएका स्थानीयले डाक्टर र नर्सलाई कुटे
articles.summary:
कालीकोटमा डाक्टर र नर्समाथि अस्पतालभित्रै हातपात भएको छ।

पताँला गाउँपालिका वडा–९ थिर्पुमा रहेको पताँला अस्पतालमा मेडिकल अफिसर डा.अली हैदर राईन र स्टाफ नर्स शान्ता गिरीमाथि आक्रमण भएको हो।

अस्पतालभित्र इन्टरनेट चलाउन आएका स्थानीय व्यक्तिहरूले शुक्रबार दिउँसो १ः५० बजेतिर आफूहरूमाथि हातपात गरेको डा.अलीले जानकारी दिए।

उनका अनुसार स्थानीय मैना बम, उनका दुई छोरा र अन्य स्थानीय समेतले आक्रमण गरेको हुन्। मैना बमका १४ र १५ वर्षका दुई छोराहरू अस्पतालको ओपीडी अगाडि बसेर मोबाइलमा भिडियो गेम खेलिरहेका थिए।

अस्पताल नजिकै घर भएकाले बमका उनीहरू वाईफाई चलाउन अस्पताल आइरहने गर्छन्। डा.अली र नर्स गिरीले उनीहरूलाई बाहिर गएर मोबाइल चलाउन भनेका थिए। त्यसो भनेपछि उनीहरू ‘यहीँ बसेर चलाउँछौँ कसले के गर्छ ?’ भनेर जङ्गिए।

त्यसपछि सुरक्षा गार्डले बाहिर निकाल्न खोज्दा उनीहरूसहित आमा मैना बम र अन्यले समेत आफूहरुलाई आक्रमण गरेको डा.अलीले बताए।

वाईफाई चलाउने बहानामा बनाएर उनीहरू नियोजित रुपमै आफूलाई आक्रमण गर्न आएको आरोप डा.अलीको छ।

articles.title: हेटौँडाको जंगलमा बोराभित्र महिलाको शव फेला
articles.summary:
मकवानपुरको हेटौँडा उपमहानगरपालिका–१५, सेल्फी रोडस्थित सामुदायिक वनमा बोरामा हालेर खाल्डोमा फालिएको अवस्थामा एक महिलाको शव भेटिएको छ।

शुक्रबार दिउँसो स्थानीयवासी च्याउ टिप्न जंगल पुगेका बेला सेतो बोरामा बाँधेर खाल्डोमा फालिएको शव देखेपछि प्रहरीलाई खबर गरेका थिए।

जिल्ला प्रहरी कार्यालय मकवानपुरका प्रवक्ता डीएसपी माधवप्रसाद काफ्लेका अनुसार सूचना पाएलगत्तै इलाका प्रहरी कार्यालय पशुपतिनगरबाट प्रहरी निरीक्षक किशोर आचार्यको नेतृत्वमा टोली घटनास्थल पुगेको थियो।

घटनास्थल सुरक्षित राखेर थप अनुसन्धानका लागि जिल्ला प्रहरी कार्यालयबाट प्रहरी उपरीक्षक श्यामबहादुर खत्रीको नेतृत्वमा तालिमप्राप्त कुकुरसहितको टोली पनि परिचालन गरिएको काफ्लेले बताए।

प्रहरीका अनुसार बोराभित्र अन्दाजी ३० देखि ३२ वर्ष उमेरकी जस्तो देखिने महिलाको शव फेला परेको हो। मृतकको नाम, थर र ठेगाना भने अहिलेसम्म खुल्न सकेको छैन।

कानुनी प्रक्रिया पूरा गरी शव हेटौँडा अस्पतालमा ल्याइएको छ। घटनाको प्रकृति र मृतकको पहिचान खुलाउने विषयमा थप अनुसन्धान भइरहेको प्रहरीले जनाएको छ।

articles.title: एआईले पहिलो पटक बनायो नयाँ भाइरस
articles.summary:
अमेरिकाका वैज्ञानिकहरूले कृत्रिम बुद्धिमत्ता (एआई) को प्रयोग गरेर प्रकृतिमा पहिले कहिल्यै नभेटिएका नयाँ भाइरसहरू सिर्जना गरेका छन्।

यो उपलब्धिलाई चिकित्सा क्षेत्रमा ठूलो प्रगतिको रूपमा हेरिएको छ। तर, यसले जैविक सुरक्षासम्बन्धी नयाँ चिन्ता पनि थपेको छ।

यो अध्ययन प्रतिष्ठित साइन्स जर्नलमा प्रकाशित भएको हो। स्ट्यानफोर्ड विश्वविद्यालय तथा एमआईटी–हार्वर्डको ब्रोड इन्स्टिच्युटका अनुसन्धानकर्ताहरूले ब्याक्टेरियालाई मात्र संक्रमित गर्ने ‘फेज’ नामक भाइरसलाई आधार बनाएर एआईमार्फत हजारौं नयाँ जीनोम डिजाइन गरेका थिए।

तीमध्ये करिब ३०० जीनोम प्रयोगशालामा रासायनिक रूपमा तयार गरी परीक्षण गर्दा १६ वटा नयाँ भाइरस सफलतापूर्वक काम गर्न सक्षम भएको पाइएको छ।

अनुसन्धानका अनुसार यी एआईबाट बनाइएका केही भाइरसहरूले ई. कोलाई ब्याक्टेरियालाई प्राकृतिक भाइरसभन्दा अझ प्रभावकारी रूपमा नष्ट गरेका थिए। वैज्ञानिकहरूका अनुसार भविष्यमा यस्ता फेजहरू एन्टिबायोटिकले काम नगर्ने संक्रमणको उपचारमा उपयोगी हुन सक्छन्।

तर विज्ञहरूले यो प्रविधिको दुरुपयोग हुन सक्ने जोखिमबारे पनि चेतावनी दिएका छन्।

टोरन्टो विश्वविद्यालयका संक्रामक रोग विशेषज्ञ आइज्याक बोगोचले एआईबाट डिजाइन गरिएका भाइरसहरूले औषधि प्रतिरोधी ब्याक्टेरियाविरुद्ध नयाँ उपचारको बाटो खोल्न सक्ने बताए। तर, यही प्रविधि हानिकारक रोगजनक बनाउन प्रयोग भए गम्भीर जैविक सुरक्षा चुनौती उत्पन्न हुन सक्ने उनको भनाइ छ।

अष्ट्रेलियाको सिड्नीस्थित वैज्ञानिक फतेमेह वाफाईका अनुसार यस अध्ययनमा प्रयोग गरिएका फेज भाइरसले मानिसलाई संक्रमित गर्दैनन्। तर, एआईले भाइरस डिजाइन गर्न सक्ने क्षमता देखिएकाले भविष्यमा कडा सुरक्षा मापदण्ड आवश्यक पर्ने उनले बताइन्।

यता बेलायतको एआई सेक्युरिटी इन्स्टिच्युटले हालै केही अत्याधुनिक एआई मोडेलहरूले सुरक्षा परीक्षणका क्रममा स्वायत्त रूपमा दुर्भावनापूर्ण गतिविधि गरेको जनाएको छ। यसले एआईको सुरक्षित प्रयोगबारे विश्वभर थप बहस सुरु भएको छ।

यद्यपि, इम्पेरियल कलेज लन्डनका विज्ञ टम एलिसका अनुसार अहिलेको उपलब्धि मुख्यतः साना र सरल फेज भाइरसमा सीमित छ। कोभिड–१९ जस्ता जटिल भाइरस बनाउन अहिलेको एआई अझ धेरै टाढा रहेको उनले बताए।

सिंगापुरस्थित एसिया सेन्टर फर हेल्थ सेक्युरिटीका निर्देशक ह्सु ली याङले पनि एआईको क्षमताबारे अनावश्यक डर फैलाउनु नहुने बताए।

एआईको सहायताले जो–कोहीले सजिलै खतरनाक भाइरस बनाउन सक्ने अवस्था अहिले नभएको बताउँदै उनले त्यसका लागि उच्चस्तरीय प्रयोगशाला र विशेषज्ञता अझै पनि आवश्यक पर्ने बताए।

यस अनुसन्धानले भविष्यमा नयाँ उपचार विकास गर्ने सम्भावना देखाएको छ। तर, त्यही प्रविधिको दुरुपयोग रोक्न कडा जैविक सुरक्षा, निगरानी र स्पष्ट नियम आवश्यक रहेकोमा अधिकांश विज्ञहरूको मत एकै छ।
